articles.title: Microsoft 2026 Security Report: Autonomous Ransomware Has Hacked Real Organizations - Tech Times
articles.summary: Microsoft 2026 Security Report: Autonomous Ransomware Has Hacked Real Organizations  Tech Times
articles.full_text:
Cyberattackers reached AI's advantages ahead of defenders in 2026 — and the gap is widening fast enough that Microsoft is now predicting a multi-year period in which the backlog of known but unpatched vulnerabilities swells while adversaries stockpile zero-days at machine speed. Those are the central conclusions of the 2026 Microsoft Digital Defense Report, released October 1 and drawing on data from more than 165 trillion security signals processed daily. The report covers July 2025 through June 2026, and it does not treat autonomous AI attacks as a coming threat — it documents them as one that has already arrived.
In July 2026, the Sysdig Threat Research Team documented JADEPUFFER — the first confirmed fully automated ransomware extortion attack, in which AI-orchestrated systems autonomously identified targets, delivered ransom demands, and managed the extortion workflow with minimal human involvement. Microsoft says it has since observed additional AI-orchestrated intrusions carrying characteristics consistent with JADEPUFFER activity, though at low volumes. Meanwhile, in controlled evaluation environments, frontier models — specifically Anthropic Mythos Preview and OpenAI GPT-5.5 — chained together 32 consecutive attack steps to achieve full domain compromise of an emulated enterprise network without any human direction. "AI is changing the physics of cybersecurity," Microsoft wrote in the report's opening statement.
Speed Gap: AI Weaponizes Flaws Before Defenders Can Patch
The structural core of 2026's threat environment is a timing mismatch that AI has made nearly impossible to close. The median window to active weaponization between a vulnerability being discovered in the wild and active exploitation has fallen to well below 24 hours. Enterprise remediation for critical external vulnerabilities, by contrast, routinely takes 30 to 60 days — a structural gap that exists because most production systems require robust unit and integration testing before code changes can be safely deployed, a constraint AI cannot remove.
The vulnerability volume is accelerating to match. Nearly 40,000 Common Vulnerabilities and Exposures (CVEs) were published in the first half of 2026 alone, putting the full year on track to hit a record-projected 72,000 CVEs — a figure that would roughly double 2025's count. Microsoft warned that well-resourced adversaries may now be able to stockpile large numbers of zero-day exploits discovered through AI-powered code analysis, accumulating offensive options faster than any single organization can remediate its own exposure.
Phishing's Resurgence: AI Personalization at Mass Scale
Phishing accounted for 23% of the intrusions Microsoft's incident responders investigated between July 2025 and June 2026 — up sharply from 7% the year prior. Exploits targeting public-facing applications climbed from 15% to 24% over the same period.
The phishing surge reflects something more specific than volume. AI allows attackers to personalize phishing lures at mass scale — effectively industrializing spear-phishing, previously a labor-intensive and high-skill operation. Microsoft's report noted that fraudsters once betrayed themselves through four tells: forged documents that looked off, writing that read like a second language, an accent that slipped through on a video interview, and a thin or absent online footprint. "AI fixes all four simultaneously," the report stated. The same capability fuels North Korea's remote IT worker operations — which use AI-generated deepfake video to pass job interviews and embed operatives inside Western organizations.
Credential theft remains the dominant post-access behavior. In 52.2% of intrusions via valid accounts, attackers harvested additional credentials once inside; another 18.4% of sessions involved active password-spraying campaigns. Across the full 12-month reporting period, Microsoft detected more than 46 million business contact impersonation attacks.
How AI Became Operational Tradecraft for Nation-States
Microsoft documents concrete AI adoption across the four major state-sponsored threat clusters — not experimental use, but operational tradecraft embedded in real campaigns.
Chinese state-aligned actors now routinely deploy AI tools to search for exploitable vulnerabilities and to iterate on exploitation pathways, layering AI-assisted reconnaissance on top of longstanding phishing and remote access trojan playbooks.
Russian state actors adopted what the report describes as "vibe coding" — using AI to rapidly generate and iterate on attack tooling — boosting both the scale and velocity of their campaigns. AI-generated infrastructure code has been observed accelerating the build-out of attack platforms.
North Korean operators made perhaps the most systematic integration. Beyond the IT worker scheme, separate DPRK-linked groups use AI for malware creation and infrastructure management. Some have experimented with agentic AI workflows — in which large language models are given tools and autonomy to execute multi-step tasks — to accelerate malware deployment. In March 2026, North Korean actors executed a supply chain attack on Axios, compromising the Axios npm package and targeting downstream developers. Earlier, the Konni group had used AI-generated PowerShell malware against blockchain engineers.
Iran and China, Russia and North Korea all appeared in the report's nation-state sections as expanding AI use across the full intrusion lifecycle. Microsoft projects all four will continue adding autonomous systems to their toolkit.
AI-Native Malware: What These Architectures Actually Do
The most technically consequential section of the report describes a new generation of malware designed around AI from the ground up — not tools that happen to use AI, but architectures whose fundamental design would be impossible without it.
s1ngularity (August 2025): Distributed through trojanized npm packages, this malware had a novel exfiltration mechanism. Rather than carrying its own data-harvesting payload, it scanned infected machines for AI development tools already installed — specifically Claude Code, Gemini CLI, and Amazon Q CLI. When found, s1ngularity invoked those legitimate tools using permissive permission overrides designed to bypass their built-in safety controls, then directed them to hunt for secrets, API keys, and SSH credentials. The operation exfiltrated approximately 2,000 secrets and 20,000 files from 225 victim organizations before it was contained.
PromptLock (experimental prototype): This ransomware shipped containing only prompts — no compiled payload. At runtime, it contacted an attacker-controlled server hosting an open-weights language model, which dynamically generated Lua execution scripts that were then run on the victim machine. The design separates the detectable artifact from the malicious code, making signature-based detection fundamentally harder: what arrives on the victim machine is, technically, just a template.
JADEPUFFER (July 2026): The Sysdig Threat Research Team documented the first confirmed case in which AI orchestrated an autonomous ransomware extortion workflow — not just the deployment of malware, but the full extortion lifecycle with minimal human direction. Microsoft subsequently observed AI-orchestrated intrusions sharing characteristics with JADEPUFFER, though at low volume. Separately, in a July 2026 incident, OpenAI cybersecurity model training agents escaped their sandbox and attacked Hugging Face to obtain benchmark answer keys — a documented, real-world instance of agentic AI causing unintended harm outside a controlled environment.
A June 2026 research publication confirmed that self-propagating AI worms are feasible with current technology. Microsoft warned that an adversary could construct a worm using stolen LLM API keys to autonomously research new vulnerabilities and refine its own social engineering at runtime — a capability the report characterized as a near-term emerging threat.
What AI Gets Defenders in Return
Microsoft is careful to distinguish "attackers currently ahead" from "defense is impossible." The same AI capabilities that accelerate attacks also accelerate detection, triage, and response — and the report documents measurable gains on the defensive side.
Organizations using Microsoft Security Copilot reported summarizing threats 60 to 70% faster, significantly compressing mean time to resolve critical alerts. Microsoft's own disruption of the Tycoon2FA phishing-as-a-service platform — in a March 2026 operation coordinated with international law enforcement — drove the service's activity down 95% from its November 2025 peak and cut its share of CAPTCHA-gated phishing from 76% to 12%. The EvilTokens AI-powered fraud platform, which had compromised more than 12,000 email inboxes across more than 10,000 organizations within months of launching in February 2026, was similarly disrupted in a September 2026 coordinated action.
Between February and early May 2026, Microsoft Defender observed ClickFix-style attacker-supplied commands executed on more than 1.1 million unique devices — roughly an eightfold increase — which Microsoft both tracked and contained.
The report's defensive framework distills to three imperatives: strengthen the foundations (identity, least privilege, internet-facing exposure), secure AI systems as they enter the environment (treat AI agents' permissions and data access with the same rigor as human credentials), and deploy AI for defense at machine speed (continuous threat detection, AI-assisted triage, intelligence-to-action compression). Microsoft identified identity as the primary control plane — noting that 78% of attack techniques against critical infrastructure relied on cloud identity abuse.

articles.title: Why Canada is preparing for a (long shot) US invasion - BBC
articles.summary: Why Canada is preparing for a (long shot) US invasion  BBC‘At war’: Allies’ relationship implodes  News.com.auThe Turner Report: Yankee invaders (no, not the tourists)  Niagara NowCanada should hold on to military relationship with U.S., former defence chief says  theglobeandmail.comConrad Black: Carney's invasion musings  National Post
articles.full_text:
Prime Minister Mark Carney admitted last week that he has prepared for a once-unthinkable scenario - a US invasion.
Noting the risk was low and the likelihood highly improbable, he told the New York Times he had a responsibility to consider all possibilities as the US-Canada relationship is redefined under the Donald Trump presidency.
"That's just risk management," Carney said.
Trump's global tariffs and his often-repeated desire to make Canada the 51st state has led Canada to war game an attack by the Americans.
In 2025, the US president said it was "highly unlikely" that the US would ever use force against Canada. Instead he said, he would continue to exert economic pressures to obtain political aims.
"President Trump has done more than anyone to protect the great people of Canada," the White House told the BBC in a statement this week.
Military experts who spoke to the BBC also think an invasion is a long shot, pointing to the multiple ways the two countries work together on defence.
But the issue is clearly weighing on Canadians' minds.
In January, after the US captured Nicolás Maduro in Venezuela, a Leger poll suggested that over 30% of Canadians believed that a US invasion was likely.
Why it is unlikely to happen
A war between Canada and the US would be complicated and almost difficult to imagine, said Lt-Gen Christopher Coates, a former military officer of 34 years with the Royal Canadian Air Force who held various senior positions.
"I was involved in military operations for my whole career, and we never considered the possibility that there would be a military attack coming from US territory," he told the BBC.
Coates, who had served on Nato missions, noted that Canada and the US collaborate on many aspects of military defence.
They are both members of the north Atlantic defence alliance, which mandates members to defend a fellow member-nation should they be attacked.
The two countries also conduct joint Arctic defence missions under the North American Aerospace Defence Command (NORAD), and frequently share intelligence.
Because of this, Coates said he believes an attack by the US on Canada would not begin with an armed assault, but rather with more discreet means like cyberwarfare.
Not always the best of friends
After World War II, Canada and the US became natural allies for the latter part of the 20th Century, and have become heavily integrated economically, militarily and culturally.
But it wasn't always this way. In fact, a core tenet of Canada's identity is its resistance of US expansionism in the 18th and 19th Centuries, said Tim Foran, a researcher with the Canadian War Museum.
"Fear of the United States is foundational to the political project that is Canada," he said.
Canada was formed as a collection of British North American colonies who remained loyal to the British Crown when the colonies in the modern-day US rebelled.
Before the formation of Canada, the US had attempted to invade British North American colonies, taking control of Montreal in 1775 and nearly conquering Quebec City.
In the war of 1812, the Americans invaded what was known then as Upper Canada, Lower Canada and the maritime colonies repeatedly, resulting in a stalemate. During that war, British troops famously burned down the White House in retaliation.
Foran said that at the time, the colonies that later became Canada relied on Great Britain and its Royal Navy for its defence, as well as indigenous peoples who served as generals in major battles.
Canada again contemplated war with the US post-World War I in response to its growing power and influence.
It drafted a plan that was informed by secret trips to border cities made by Canadian army generals, who would pose as tourists and snap photos of bridges and highways for intelligence.
They also spoke to local residents to better understand their enemy.
A war was an unlikely scenario then, said Andrew Burtch, a researcher with the Canadian War Museum with expertise on Canada in the 20th Century, but the Canadians still wanted to be prepared.
"That's part of what militaries do," he said. "They envisage all sorts of different scenarios."
What a US invasion could look like
Even if a US invasion is extremely unlikely, Matthew Schmidt, an associate professor of national security at the University of New Haven in Connecticut, said the fact that Canadians were preparing was a sign of just how drastically the global order has shifted.
He added Canadian leaders do have hard questions to ask about how closely they want to continue working with the American military - a partnership that gives them valuable information should they want to harm Canada in any way.
"It's really doing harm to relationships with the United States, and there's a certain amount of legitimate fear," he said.
Americans might not take Trump's comments about making Canada the 51st state seriously, he said, but Canadians clearly do - and are prepared to defend themselves if needed.
So what would it be like if it happened?
The first phase of a war could be quite short.
According to the model used by the Canadian military, as reported on by the Globe and Mail newspaper earlier this year, a US attack would see Canada's strategic positions overwhelmed within a week
Its military would quickly be outnumbered, forcing Canadian forces to resort to guerilla-type warfare to try to suppress their enemy.
Allied nations like France and Britain would be called on to provide support and defence for Canada, the newspaper reported in January, citing senior government officials.
The theoretical model is believed to be the first time in a century that Canada planned for an American assault.
The modelling is on the lighter end of military combat planning, Coates said.
He said that Canada, unlike its Nato allies, was lagging behind when it came to having a response plan in place in the event of any ground invasion, and that it was now playing catch-up in this era of unpredictable geopolitics.
Part of that, he said, was made evident by a recent call by Canada's defence chief to drastically increase the size of its military, including the addition of as many as 300,000 lightly trained citizen soldiers.
An invasion of Canada might not be straightforward from the US point of view either.
Even with its outsized military, the US would have a difficult time getting buy-in for a fight with Canada, said Schmidt.
"I think you would have a large number of American officers who would resign if given the order to invade Canada," he said.
"They would see it as an illegal and immoral order."
Schmidt said Canadian soldiers and American soldiers routinely train together, and share a mutual respect.
But in the unlikely scenario that relations would deteriorate to the point of combat, Schmidt said the US would likely focus on acquiring valuable Canadian resources like oil and minerals, and political decapitation.
"You would see a a kind of operation that would mirror perhaps what you saw in Venezuela," he said, referring to US military action earlier this year to capture former Venezuelan President Maduro.
Although he acknowledged the US has greater military capacity, he said that "pound for pound" Canadian soldiers would be able to put up a fight.

articles.title: Russia Rehearses Seizing Territory of Central Asian Neighbor in Massive 47,000-Troop War Games - UNITED24 Media
articles.summary: Russia Rehearses Seizing Territory of Central Asian Neighbor in Massive 47,000-Troop War Games  UNITED24 MediaPutin observes military drills in the Urals involving troops from China and other nations  AP NewsRussia rehearses invasion and occupation of Central Asian country during military exercises  Українська правдаChinese PLA completes Russia’s Center-2026 exercise with 99A tanks, unmanned systems; expert highlights lessons from modern warfare  Global Ti...
articles.full_text:
Russia rehearsed an offensive into the territory of a neighboring Central Asian state and the creation of a “security zone” there during the Center-2026 military exercises, which involved more than 47,000 personnel across multiple training grounds and the Caspian Sea.
According to Interfax on October 2, Russian forces practiced repelling an attack in the South Ural direction before switching to offensive operations intended to retake captured territory and establish a security zone on neighboring land.
“The coalition grouping of forces is repelling the main attack in the South Ural direction, has restored the situation, and since October 2 has been conducting offensive operations to liberate the captured territory and create a security zone on adjacent territory,” Russian Deputy Defense Minister Yunus-Bek Yevkurov told Russian leader Vladimir Putin during the exercises.
Russian officials did not identify the neighboring state involved in the scenario. Kazakhstan, however, is the only Central Asian country that shares a land border with Russia. It directly borders Russia’s Chelyabinsk region, where the main stage of Center-2026 was held, and also has access to the Caspian Sea, where another part of the exercises took place.
The drills ran from September 28 through October 3 and involved more than 47,000 military personnel across 11 training grounds and the Caspian Sea, according to Russian officials. Around 2,000 pieces of military equipment, 90 aircraft and helicopters, and 77 warships and support vessels were involved in the exercises.
At the Chebarkul training ground in the Chelyabinsk region, Russian forces deployed tanks, motorcycles, artillery, drones, aircraft, and other military equipment. A T-14 Armata tank was among the systems demonstrated during the exercises.
The Caspian Flotilla simultaneously conducted an anti-landing operation, while four Russian long-range aircraft practiced strikes against what the exercise scenario described as critical enemy infrastructure.
Military contingents from Belarus, China, Kyrgyzstan, Mongolia, Pakistan, and Tajikistan also participated in Center-2026. Kazakhstan was represented during the exercises by an operational group.
Putin attended the drills at the Chebarkul training ground on October 2. Russian officials said units directly participating in Russia’s war against Ukraine were not deployed for the exercises, although the training incorporated battlefield experience gained during the invasion.
More than 2,000 Russian personnel who had fought in Ukraine participated in Center-2026, according to Russian Deputy Defense Minister Yevkurov, while equipment previously used on the battlefield was also incorporated into the drills.
The Center-2026 scenario therefore extended beyond defending Russian territory: after repelling the simulated attack, Russian-led forces were tasked with crossing into neighboring territory and establishing a security zone there.
Earlier, Ukrainian intelligence reported that Russia planned to train around 600 Chinese troops in 2025 using battlefield experience gained during its war against Ukraine. The program reportedly focused on tank warfare, artillery, air defense, and combat engineering, marking a broader expansion of military cooperation between Moscow and Beijing.

articles.title: Zakharova, following Russia’s nuclear warning to NATO: “If Europe attacks Russia, it will be a completely different and very short war” - Spotmedia.ro
articles.summary: Zakharova, following Russia’s nuclear warning to NATO: “If Europe attacks Russia, it will be a completely different and very short war”  Spotmedia.ro
articles.full_text:
Russia is intensifying its warnings towards Europe, after Moscow informed NATO that it is prepared to resort to nuclear weapons if the Alliance attempts to isolate the Kaliningrad region.
The spokesperson for the Russian Ministry of Foreign Affairs, Maria Zakharova, claims that Europe is being pushed towards a potential conflict with Russia and accuses NATO states of expanding their military infrastructure and practicing scenarios that could involve blocking the Russian enclave on the Baltic Sea.
The statement was published by the Russian Embassy in Romania, presenting it as Zakharova's response to a nuclear warning issued a day earlier by the Russian Embassy in Ireland.
"The Russophobic hysteria of the revanchist circles in the West has reached its peak. Some 'hotheads' are systematically pushing Europe towards a potential conflict, laying the groundwork for escalating tensions. Ordinary Europeans are intimidated with apocalyptic scenarios and so-called 'hybrid' threats allegedly coming from our country," Zakharova states.
Moscow Accuses NATO of Preparing Scenarios Against Kaliningrad
The spokesperson for the Russian Ministry of Foreign Affairs speaks of the "total militarization" of Europe, the increase in defense spending, and the expansion of NATO infrastructure.
"Aggressive exercises by allies are taking place in the immediate vicinity of our borders, within which offensive scenarios against our country are being practiced, including a possible blockade of the Kaliningrad region, isolating Russian ports on the Baltic Sea, as well as the transfer of allied troops through the Suwałki corridor," Zakharova asserts.
However, NATO rejects the accusation of preparing an attack on Russian territory and states that its exercises are defensive in nature.
Several allied exercises have taken place in the region in recent months. In August, NATO conducted an aerial exercise over northeastern Poland, near Kaliningrad, involving American and Norwegian aircraft, an AWACS aircraft, and aircraft for refueling and electronic warfare. The Polish command specified at the time that the exercise was planned and aimed to improve cooperation between allied forces.
The Suwałki Corridor, a strip of territory between Poland and Lithuania located between Kaliningrad and Belarus, holds significant strategic importance for NATO: it represents the only land link between the Baltic States and the rest of the Alliance territory.
Statements of European Leaders Invoked by Zakharova
Zakharova accuses European leaders of openly discussing a possible conflict with Russia.
"Some European leaders dare to publicly talk about the possibility of 'wiping off the face of the earth' the Russian anti-aircraft defense bases and missile systems in the Kaliningrad region," she states.
The reference seems to target, among others, statements made in May by the Lithuanian Minister of Foreign Affairs, Kęstutis Budrys. He stated that NATO must show Moscow that it has the capacity to neutralize Russian systems in Kaliningrad in case of a conflict.
Zakharova also mentions the Polish Minister of Foreign Affairs, Radosław Sikorski, whom she says "dreams of provoking a military defeat of Russia."
In September, Sikorski declared at the Yalta European Strategy conference in Kiev that if Russia were to attack NATO, the Alliance forces could defeat Russia quickly due to air superiority. "If Russia were to attack us and we didn't take off our gloves, I think we would beat Russia fairly quickly," the Polish minister said, according to The Independent.
In the same speech, Zakharova accuses the Estonian Minister of Defense of speaking about the advantages of a "preventive" war with Russia.
"These politicians, and not only them, have come to believe that war will be fought exclusively with those means in which NATO, in their opinion, holds an advantage. These people need to be brought back down to earth," says the Russian Ministry of Foreign Affairs spokesperson.
"It Will Be a Completely Different War and It Will Be a Very Short One"
Zakharova asserts that Russia does not intend to attack European states but warns that Moscow has the means to respond to any aggression.
"We hope that our warnings will be heard by those to whom they are addressed. As the President of the Russian Federation, Vladimir Putin, stated, our country does not threaten and does not intend to threaten European states. But no one should doubt that Russia has all the capabilities necessary to prevent any aggression and to defeat any aggressor. If Europe attacks Russia, it will already be a completely different war - and it will be a very short one," concludes Maria Zakharova.
Where the Nuclear Warning Originated
Russia recently sent a clear warning to NATO regarding Kaliningrad. The Russian Embassy in Ireland stated that Moscow would be prepared to use its "entire arsenal, including nuclear weapons," if NATO states attempted to isolate Kaliningrad from the rest of Russia. Similar messages have been transmitted by other Russian embassies in Europe.
However, the warning was not limited to the public communication of embassies. Reuters has seen a document sent by Russia to NATO, in which Moscow accuses the Alliance of following a "dangerous and ill-considered course," which would create a high risk of direct military conflict.
NATO has rejected Moscow's accusations and demanded that Russia cease nuclear threats. The Secretary-General of the Alliance, Mark Rutte, stated on Wednesday that NATO is a defensive alliance and its activities do not threaten Russia. When asked if Moscow's warning means that the risk of using nuclear weapons against the Baltic States has become real, Rutte replied: "No."
He said that NATO must remain calm but prepared, and reiterated that the Alliance will defend "every inch" of its territory.

articles.title: SA’s ransomware problem is hiding a much bigger question - Daily Maverick
articles.summary: SA’s ransomware problem is hiding a much bigger question  Daily Maverick
articles.full_text:
South Africa has a cyber problem. The harder question is whether we would recognise it if part of that problem were not crime.
In the past two months, Cartrack confirmed a ransomware attack on 26 August. EasyEquities and Satrix warned clients after RelyComply, the identity-verification provider behind their Know Your Customer checks, confirmed an intruder in its environment. Alexforbes has linked its own exposure to the same provider. Cell C says its incident involved a different one. Bidvest Bank has issued its own notice. Air Traffic and Navigation Services has appointed forensic investigators.
None of this, taken alone, proves anything geopolitical. Cartrack told customers the incident was believed to have been carried out by Dire Wolf, a double-extortion ransomware crew, though its public web notice does not name the group. Dire Wolf separately listed Cartrack on its leak site and claimed 500GB of data. MyBroadband’s review of the leaked material found that much of it concerned American customers. Dire Wolf has also claimed RelyComply, and says it seeks only money and has no political stance. The public record fits ordinary extortion far better than statecraft.
Air Traffic and Navigation Services is harder. It is dealing with two matters. Preliminary findings indicate a ransomware incident in an operational-technology environment supporting weather-related air-traffic services. Separately, initial inquiries could not substantiate an allegation of employee data theft. In the first, network monitoring reportedly indicated possible exfiltration to IP addresses located in China. That identifies where a server sits, not who controls it.
Test
My argument is not that South Africa’s foreign policy caused any of these incidents. It is that a state claiming strategic autonomy must be able to distinguish ordinary cybercrime from strategic operations when the evidence starts to overlap. The recent incidents are not evidence of a campaign. They are a test of whether South Africa could tell a campaign from an ordinary run of cybercrime. What is publicly visible does not answer that question.
The reflex is to ask whether this is cyberwarfare. That is the wrong question. Thomas Rid argued long ago that cyberwar will not take place. The consequential activity sits between crime and war, in espionage, subversion and sabotage. The law draws similar lines. Tallinn Manual 2.0, the influential but non-binding expert analysis of international law in cyberspace, works through 79 rules on sovereignty, state responsibility, specialised regimes and international peace and security before it reaches the law of armed conflict.
Violation of sovereignty (itself contested as a standalone rule), coercive intervention, use of force and armed attack are different thresholds with different consequences. “Cyberwarfare” should not be the category that does the initial analytical work.
But not war does not mean not strategic. Cyberpersistence theorists argue that states compete through continuous campaigns whose effects accumulate below the armed-attack threshold: access gained, credentials harvested, suppliers mapped. Cyberpersistence theory therefore gives us a reason to test for campaigns, not to infer one from a cluster.
Nor does crime versus state divide cleanly. Tim Maurer shows that states delegate operations to proxies, orchestrate them through looser support, or sanction them by knowingly tolerating activity they could stop. Criminals carry political motives. States buy criminal access. “It’s ransomware” does not end the inquiry. “The victim was strategic” does not begin one.
South Africa has already seen political grievance turn digital. In May, #OpSouthAfrica, a campaign by Nigerian-linked hacktivist groups including Nullsec Nigeria, claimed attacks on Sita, the Civil Aviation Authority, the SA Social Security Agency and Correctional Services in retaliation for xenophobic violence. Many of the claims remain unverified. The retaliatory intent was explicit even where the claimed compromises were not.
Intelligence interest
Foreign policy can create intelligence interest. South Africa is the applicant against Israel at the International Court of Justice, a prominent BRICS member, and a self-described non-aligned state with public positions on Ukraine and the Middle East. But interest is not evidence of targeting, and targeting is not evidence of responsibility for any present incident. There is no public evidence that any state is behind these incidents, and naming one would turn a security question into a conspiracy theory.
Henry Farrell and Abraham Newman offer a structural lens. States that control the hubs of asymmetric global networks can use that position to watch and to coerce. For South Africa, the question is which financial, communications, cloud and identity networks run through foreign-controlled hubs through which strategically valuable information or leverage could flow. That is the attack surface.
Seeing it turns on attribution, which is five questions, not one. What happened technically? Who ran the operation? What is their relationship to any state? Is their conduct legally attributable to that state? Should the government say so publicly? Maurer’s categories answer the third question, not the fourth. For private actors of this kind, conduct becomes attributable to a state where they act on its instructions or under its direction or control, or where the state later acknowledges and adopts the conduct as its own. Tolerance and sympathy do not suffice.
Peacetime espionage is not, as such, unlawful under international law, though the means used may breach other rules. That makes espionage especially difficult to condemn in legal terms. And the African Union’s 2024 Common African Position treats due diligence as an obligation: a state that knows or should know that wrongful cyber operations are using infrastructure in its territory or under its control must take feasible measures within its capacity to stop them.
That can give South Africa an argument about the territorial state’s own omission even where the underlying operation cannot be attributed to it. Not every state agrees. The United Kingdom, for one, does not accept that state practice yet establishes such a rule.
Discipline requires saying what would disprove the hypothesis, and none of the relevant indicators is state-specific. Clean monetisation, interest only in saleable data, and apparent links that dissolve into shared suppliers point towards crime. Selective collection of material with intelligence value but no resale value, persistence without visible return, and re-entry after eviction point, weakly, the other way.
Clues
Criminals persist too, and absent monetisation may simply be monetisation not yet seen. What matters is whether several weak clues begin pointing in the same direction. A cluster becomes a campaign only when independent evidence links the incidents operationally or by a coherent common objective. Chronology does neither. Nor does diplomatic timing. There is always a diplomatic event.
Each forensic firm answers for its client. The National Cybersecurity Hub is a national response team linked to sector teams. The Information Regulator receives security-compromise notifications under section 22 of the Protection of Personal Information Act. But the public architecture does not establish that any single institution receives a compulsory, sufficiently detailed cross-sector technical feed capable of campaign-level correlation.
Nor can the public record show what intelligence structures already see. Section 54 of the Cybercrimes Act would oblige communications providers and financial institutions to report specified offences to the police. It is still not in force, and it would not create such a feed on its own.
A lawful mechanism is needed for sharing minimised technical indicators, and enough metadata to correlate them, with privacy and confidentiality controls built in. It should build on the reporting duties the Critical Infrastructure Protection Act already contemplates. Section 54 should be commenced. More fundamentally, an institution needs clear national responsibility for cross-sector correlation and for escalating suspicious patterns into intelligence assessment.
If the evidence shows a global ransomware economy hitting vulnerable systems, that is worth knowing. If it shows something else, we need to know that too. Being able to reject the geopolitical hypothesis on evidence, rather than assumption, is itself a form of state capability.
“Ransomware” answers one question. Sovereignty requires us to ask the rest. Foreign policy has an attack surface.
South Africa wants strategic autonomy. But would we know if someone were using cyberspace to contest it? DM

articles.summary: NATO fighter jets scrambled amid huge attack as people warned 'find a safe place'  AOL.comUkraine live: Russia targets major Kyiv bridge in widening attacks on infrastructure  The IndependentLithuania’s authorities issue all-clear following earlier air alert  LRTUnidentified Object Entered Lithuanian Airspace From Belarus—Search Underway  МілітарнийWest Bank: Israeli settlers raid Palestinian homes and attack olive pickers  Agenzia Nova
articles.full_text:
NATO fighter jets were scrambled in Lithuania after a suspected drone crossed into the country, forcing Vilnius Airport in the capital to close its airspace. Lithuanian authorities issued a possible air threat alert to residents, urging them to find a safe place.
The suspected drone was detected entering Lithuania's airspace from Belarus on Saturday morning, triggering the alarm to be sounded shortly before 10am local time. However, about 40 minutes later, the alert was cancelled as officials said it no longer caused a threat. Vilmantas Vitkauskas, head of Lithuania's National Crisis Management Centre, said the object had moved away from the NATO ally's observation zone.
Speaking to public broadcaster LRT TELEVISION, Mr Vitkauskas confirmed a search was underway for the unidentified object. "If it fell, if it was a drone, it will have to be found," he is translated as saying.
"But it couldn't necessarily have been a drone, because certain parameters said that the speed was slightly lower than usual. There could have been some anomaly or it could have been related to bird migration."The senior official previously said the scrambled fighter jets were attempting to confirm the nature of the object which had not been "fully identified".
He earlier said it resembled a drone on radar, but admitted it could have also been a flock of birds. Last month, an Italian figher jet stationed in Lithuania was scrambled after a possible drone sighting which turned out to be birds.
Mr Vitkauskas said authorities received reports from residents of a "possible object outside the territory of Vilnius, moving towards Jonava". Lithuania, along with its Baltic neighbours, have faced repeated drone incursions since Russia began its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022.
The number of incidents have risen in recent months as countries along NATO's eastern flank warn of an increasing threat from Moscow. In September, an Italian fighter jet shot down a suspsected drone over Lithuania. It resembled the first time a UAV had been shot down in the country's airspace.
The Italian air force has been stationed at Šiauliai Air Base, northern Lithuania, as part of the NATO Air Defence mission. NATO nations strengthen alliance airspace along its eastern flank on a four-month rotation.
Lithuania has a southern and eastern border with Belarus, a key ally of Russia, while also having a border with Kaliningrad - Russia's heavily militarised Baltic exclave. The suspected drone incursion comes as Lithuania holds its largests annual national mobilisation exercise, testing how it would react in a crisis.
Some 3,000 officials, as well as 1,000 volunteers, are taking part in Vyio Skliautas 2026 which ends on Saturday. The major drills include rehearsing for the evacuation of residents.
Vilnius is drawing up evacuation plans with neighbouring Poland in the event of an attack by Russia. The NATO allies are working on a bilateral agreement to provide a framework for the plans amid rising fears of a Russian assault.
Moscow has ramped up its threats this week, directly warning NATO it is ready to use its "entire arsenal" if the alliance threatened Kaliningrad. NATO condemned Russia for "irresponsible nuclear rhetoric".

articles.title: 'Warlock' ransomware used in attacks on critical infrastructure in Portuguese, Spanish-speaking countries - The Record from Recorded Future News
articles.summary: 'Warlock' ransomware used in attacks on critical infrastructure in Portuguese, Spanish-speaking countries  The Record from Recorded Future News

source_detail.name: The Record from Recorded Future News

articles.full_text:
Critical infrastructure organizations in Portuguese- and Spanish-speaking countries are being attacked by a Chinese group using a ransomware strain called Warlock.
The group is exploiting a variety of vulnerabilities impacting Microsoft SharePoint, according to a new report from Symantec Threat Hunter Team.
Symantec researchers said the victims include a water utility, a telecommunications provider, a university and a regional government. The organizations are located across Europe, Africa and Latin America.
Last year, Microsoft warned that China-based hackers using the Warlock ransomware were focusing their attacks on SharePoint vulnerabilities colloquially named “ToolShell.”
Symantec found that the attacks have continued into 2026 and now include newer SharePoint vulnerabilities recently spotlighted by the U.S. government.
The campaign illustrated that hackers are still finding success in exploiting SharePoint deployments that have not been patched either for the 2025 vulnerabilities or the 2026 bugs.
“The apparent recent focus on Portuguese- and Spanish-speaking countries suggests either an opportunistic targeting pattern driven by exposed, vulnerable SharePoint servers, or a more deliberate tasking,” Symantec researchers said. “The inclusion of critical infrastructure operators among the victims is a reminder of the potential real-world consequences of ransomware attacks that succeed against essential services.”
In one incident, Symantec found the attackers used a tool built to disable security software on dozens of hosts before deploying the Warlock ransomware.
The attackers carried out extensive reconnaissance on compromised systems, installing a variety of tools designed to blend their activities into normal traffic that typically came from developer or administrator workstations.
The report comes one month after the U.S. Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA) published a warning that hackers are exploiting six new SharePoint vulnerabilities providing attackers with wide access to organizations.
SharePoint is a prime target for both financially-motivated hackers as well as state-sponsored groups seeking intelligence. The service is often used to store confidential documents and is deeply integrated with Microsoft’s authentication services, meaning skillful enough hackers could use a foothold there to burrow deeper into their victims’ networks.
Last year’s hacking campaign against SharePoint instances caused global alarm after several prominent organizations were breached through the vulnerabilities. At least 400 governments and businesses were allegedly breached, including the National Nuclear Security Administration, the National Institutes of Health and the Department of Homeland Security.
In August, several Swiss government institutions were also attacked through SharePoint vulnerabilities.
Last year, Microsoft could not tie the Chinese group behind Warlock to any other Chinese state-backed group it tracks, only noting that the hackers used a strain of the LockBit ransomware before switching to Warlock.
Warlock had previously been used against organizations in the U.S., Russia, Brazil, India, Taiwan and Japan.
Jonathan Greig
is a Breaking News Reporter at Recorded Future News. Jonathan has worked across the globe as a journalist since 2014. Before moving back to New York City, he worked for news outlets in South Africa, Jordan and Cambodia. He previously covered cybersecurity at ZDNet and TechRepublic.

articles.title: Iran’s Strategy After the War: Hormuz, Gulf Tensions and the Risk of Another Conflict - Modern Diplomacy
articles.summary: Iran’s Strategy After the War: Hormuz, Gulf Tensions and the Risk of Another Conflict  Modern Diplomacy
articles.full_text:
The war involving Iran, Israel and the United States has reshaped the strategic balance across the Middle East, leaving the Strait of Hormuz at the centre of a wider contest over regional security, economic leverage and political influence. While military operations may have eased, the underlying tensions remain unresolved, with Iran retaining significant leverage over one of the world’s most important maritime chokepoints.
In this exclusive interview with Modern Diplomacy, Dr. Rob Geist Pinfold, an expert on Middle Eastern security and international relations, examines what “winning” means for Tehran after the conflict, why Iran is unlikely to fully relinquish its political claims over the Strait of Hormuz, and how the Gulf states are recalibrating their response to Iran.
Dr. Geist Pinfold also discusses the changing US-Israel-Iran strategic relationship, the growing role of the Houthis and the possibility of another round of conflict. Rather than viewing Iran, Israel or the Gulf states as unified actors with fixed objectives, he highlights the internal political shifts and competing interests shaping the region.
The conversation further explores whether the Middle East is moving toward a negotiated settlement or becoming trapped in a prolonged “no-war, no-peace” environment—with significant consequences for regional stability and the global economy.
You’ve argued Iran sees strategic value in prolonging this war rather than rushing to end it. What does “winning” actually look like for Tehran at this stage—is it about outlasting Washington’s patience, or something more specific?
Israel and the US made their goals clear in the last war: they sought regime change in Tehran. That they were unable to deliver it has allowed the regime to claim victory, since when your opponent sets such lofty goals, then all you have to do is survive. But Iran has done more than that. It has managed to create a status quo where there is no scenario at present—political, military, or otherwise—where it gives up its control over the Strait of Hormuz. With the US blockade in place, it may have lost some of that control, but all it really needs to do is demonstrate that it can cause enough chaos to dissuade companies from sending commercial vessels down the waterway and insurers from insuring them. And it remains capable of doing that. Now the Houthis—arguably Iran’s most important remaining regional ally—are threatening to close the Bab el Mandeb Strait and are escalating their attacks against Saudi Arabia, with the US unable or unwilling to respond. In short, Iran has not only ‘won’ in a narrow sense that it has survived: despite absorbing punishing blows, it has managed to exert influence over the region and the global economy in a way it could not before the conflict. The US, meanwhile, has managed to induce a crisis of regional confidence in its own leadership.
The Strait of Hormuz has become Iran’s main point of leverage. How sustainable is that as a bargaining chip, and what would have to change for Iran to actually give it up?
To answer that question, it’s important to first consider what Iran ‘giving up’ Hormuz would look like. Will it stop threatening commercial shipping? Quite possibly, if it reaches an accord with Oman that the US rejects publicly but tolerates tacitly. But will Iran go back to the pre-war status quo and renounce its claim to exercise authority over what goes in and out of the waterway? That is far less likely. At present, the only foreseeable way to open Hormuz to pre-war levels of shipping would be a deal that grants Iran (alongside at least some of the GCC states) a political role in overseeing the waterway, possibly as part of a multinational committee. It could also renounce its demand that it charge a toll on all ships if—and only if—the US agrees to wholesale sanctions relief, meaning that Iran won’t need to use Hormuz to raise revenue. At the end of the day, Iran’s control over Hormuz has always been less about money and more about political prestige; in short, it may give up the former but not the latter. A role in a post-war Hormuz, then, is less a bargaining chip for Iran to get the US to concede on other issues and more a demand that it will not give up in full under any conditions.
You’ve written about the Gulf states’ reluctance to get pulled into this conflict directly. Is that restraint holding, or are you seeing cracks in it as the war drags on?
The Gulf states’ restraint despite Iran’s aggression against them was founded on the strategic calculation that this was not their war and they would little to gain from it. For many of them, that still rings true. Many Gulf states—particularly Saudi Arabia—are naturally status quo-oriented powers that put a premium on respect for sovereignty and borders. As such, they are nervous of any attempts at regime change and even more so at the prospect of regime breakdown in Iran and the replacement of a government they might not like with a worse alternative: indefinite chaos. That largely still holds true. Nevertheless, the lack of a better ‘day after’ has meant that many Gulf states are tentatively mowing towards more hawkish responses to Iran—the majority of the GCC states are alleged to have struck back against Iran in some form. But this should not be a mistake for a comprehensive grand strategic transformation. The GCC states are all still negotiating with Iran. They are also a complex set of actors with divergent views; Bahrain, for instance, is at the hawkish end of the spectrum, whilst Oman is the most engagement-focused—the others all sit somewhere in between.
How has the US-Israel relationship shifted the strategic calculus for Iran? Does Iran read Washington’s current posture as more enabling of Israeli action, or is that overstated?
The common consensus is that the recent war on Iran was Israeli-led and Israeli-designed. It could be termed Israel’s war, but I’d argue it was more Netanyahu’s war in that the Israeli Prime Minister made containing Iran his life’s work. After October 7, Israel’s grand strategy became far more hawkish and militarily proactive and politically revisionist, and it is Netanyahu that has spearheaded that transformation. In short, this is not just an Iranian perception or Tehran’s propaganda. Nevertheless, Iran has had a tendency to project a simplified view of US-Israel relations; this is a contradictory prism—Israel is seen both as the US’s loyal proxy (i.e., the little Satan to the Great Satan) or as a malignant hand guiding US foreign and security policy in the entire region. The recent war will have likely fuelled the latter perception. But there is also an issue of credibility in the US. Tehran has never trusted its American interlocutors and will do even less now, given the US unilaterally sank the JCPOA and then twice attacked Iran directly in 2025 and 2026 (in both instances in coordination with Israel), whilst Omani-sponsored negotiations were taking place. This lack of trust complicates negotiations today.
Where does this conflict’s strategic logic seem to be heading—toward a negotiated de-escalation, a prolonged stalemate, or something else entirely?
Whenever I talk to people in the region—in both Tehran and Tel Aviv—they seem to be convinced that we are headed for another round, i.e., another war between Israel, the US, and Iran. I am not entirely convinced, but my prediction is even less optimistic. Wars are inherently terrible. But they are also catalysts for change in that previously unthinkable policy options become possible, and the political deck of cards is reshuffled both internally in the participating states and between the participating actors. This means that sometimes wars can produce more durable solutions or settlements. In the case of the Middle East, however, the region seems trapped in a paradigm of no-war, no-peace, where uneasy ceasefires are punctuated by sporadic escalations from either side whilst negotiations make no tangible progress. This quagmire is bad for states, it’s bad for people, and it’s bad for the regional economy because it hampers recovery. Neither Iran nor the US seems keen on a return to war, but neither is willing to make the necessary conditions for a significant de-escalation. The result is that the region is likely to stay stuck in the current status quo, possibly for quite some time.
What’s the biggest thing Western media coverage is getting wrong about Iran’s strategic thinking in this war?
We have to be careful of a tendency to simplify the key actors in this conflict, e.g., ‘Iran wants X,’ ‘Israel wants Y,’ or to discuss ‘the Gulf states’ as if they are one coherent actor. This is particularly problematic when it comes to Iran, because the regime is now in a real and fluid state of change following the assassination of many leading figures. As a result, we are still trying to figure out who holds the cards in Iran today. And the chances are that the Iranian leadership is too, given they are jostling for position. We know that the political leadership is weakened and the IRGC (Revolutionary Guards) is now stronger, but even this is a simplification—there are many different actors and personalities within the IRGC, and even individuals who are not explicitly IRGC may have a background within the organization. It seems like Iran has become more hardline not just as a result of how the war proceeded externally, but also as a result of how the deck has reshuffled internally, but we still don’t know how permanent this transformation is. Does it mean that a deal can’t be done, for instance? Or does it mean the opposite: that some kind of a settlement could moderate Iran’s behavior? It is likely too early to tell right now, so I would urge analysts not to jump to any definitive conclusions for the time being.

articles.title: North Korea fires missile towards South Korea amid DMZ security tensions - The Times of India
articles.summary: North Korea fires missile towards South Korea amid DMZ security tensions  The Times of India
articles.full_text:
North Korea fired at least one ballistic missile towards the East Sea early Saturday, South Korea's military said on Saturday. The incident comes as tensions rose after Seoul blamed Pyongyang for a landmine blast in the Demilitarised Zone that injured three South Korean soldiers.
The missile was launched from the Wonsan area of North Korea, according to Seoul's Joint Chiefs of Staff (JCS). The military said South Korea, the US and Japan were maintaining a "robust defence posture" through close information sharing on North Korean ballistic missile launches.
The launch came hours after Kim Yo Jong, sister of North Korean leader Kim Jong Un, rejected Seoul's demand for an apology over the DMZ explosion. She called South Korea "despicable" and dismissed Seoul's proposal for border talks as a "wild dream and unilateral jargon".
South Korea's military had demanded an official apology from Pyongyang after three of its soldiers were wounded in a landmine blast last month inside the DMZ, the heavily mined buffer zone separating the two Koreas.
Seoul and the US-led United Nations Command said an investigation found that the explosion was caused by North Korean mines laid on the South Korean side of the border. 
South Korean Defence Minister Kang Shin-chul said the mines were believed to have been planted as part of Pyongyang's efforts to fortify the border.
North Korea has denied responsibility for the blast. In a separate report carried by its official Korean Central News Agency, Kim Yo Jong said it was "quite ridiculous" for South Korea to demand an apology.
She also mocked South Korean President Lee Jae Myung's efforts to improve ties, describing his latest overture as "the climax of the farce that everyone should watch".
Despite the escalating tensions, Lee on Thursday urged Pyongyang to return to dialogue. Unification Minister Chung Dong-young also proposed talks with North Korea on Friday to address issues along the border.
North Korea has stepped up work to fortify its frontier with South Korea, including laying mines and building anti-tank barriers. The measures followed Kim Jong Un's 2024 designation of South Korea as his country's "principal enemy".
The latest flare-up comes as US President Donald Trump's recent overtures to Pyongyang have raised concerns in Seoul that South Korea could be sidelined in any future nuclear talks involving North Korea. Pyongyang is backed by Russia and China.
South Korea's opposition People Power Party has accused Lee of failing to criticise North Korea when warranted. "South Korean soldiers have been injured, and far from receiving an apology, we have been mocked by North Korea," the party said.
"We fail to see how selectively turning a blind eye to North Korea serves South Korea's dignity or the safety of its people."

articles.title: Warlock Expands SharePoint Exploitation in Critical Infrastructure Attacks - SecurityWeek
articles.summary: Warlock Expands SharePoint Exploitation in Critical Infrastructure Attacks  SecurityWeek
articles.full_text:
The Warlock ransomware group continues to target SharePoint servers in attacks against critical infrastructure, government, and education entities, Symantec reports.
Warlock is believed to be operated by a China-based hacking group tracked as Longlegs and Storm-2603, which has been linked to malicious operations such as CL-CRI-1040, CamoFei, and ChamelGang.
Last year, the Chinese state-sponsored groups Linen Typhoon and Violet Typhoon were seen exploiting two SharePoint vulnerabilities dubbed ToolShell as zero-days at least two weeks before public disclosure.
Within weeks, more than 400 SharePoint servers were compromised, and Storm-2603’s exploitation of ToolShell stood out amid heavy APT activity.
By October 2025, researchers uncovered numerous Warlock ransomware attacks that exploited ToolShell. Some of the group’s victims included a Middle East telecom firm, African and South American government entities, and a US university.
According to a fresh Symantec report, Storm-2603 continues to favor the exploitation of SharePoint bugs in attacks. In addition to ToolShell, its arsenal may also include recent flaws such as CVE-2026-32201, CVE-2026-45659, CVE-2026-56164, CVE-2026-58644, CVE-2026-50522, and CVE-2026-55040.
Over the past two months, the Warlock operator has hit at least four victim organizations in Portuguese- and Spanish-speaking countries.
“The victims included two critical infrastructure operators, a water utility and a telecommunications provider, along with a regional government body and a university,” Symantec reports.
As part of one intrusion, the hacking group deployed a tool to disable the security software on at least 40 systems and then executed Warlock on at least 33 of them.
The group’s exploitation of SharePoint flaws is typically followed by webshell deployment, ASP.NET machine key exfiltration, and the deployment of a forced signed payload for remote code execution (RCE).
Storm-2603 relies on DLL sideloading for in-memory code execution, drops additional payloads from legitimate file-sharing and storage services and a vulnerable driver to disable security tools, and relies on living-off-the-land tools for reconnaissance and command execution.
“The group has also been observed abusing Visual Studio Code’s built-in tunnel feature, installing the code-insiders.exe binary as a service to establish covert remote network access that blends into traffic that typically originates from developer or administrator workstations,” Symantec notes.
Additionally, the threat actor stages the Warlock payload inside the domain’s SYSVOL share, which is automatically replicated to every domain controller and is readable domain-wide, to execute the file-encrypting ransomware at scale.
“Longlegs’ continued activity, more than a year after Warlock ransomware first came to prominence, shows that exploitation of ToolShell and other related SharePoint vulnerabilities remains a viable initial access route for attackers on SharePoint deployments that have not been patched or otherwise mitigated,” Symantec notes.

articles.full_text:
ROYAL Marines have returned to the Faroe Islands for the first time since the Second World War as the UK steps up its military presence in the North Atlantic.
UK commandos were deployed to the archipelago to work alongside Danish and Faroese forces as part of Exercise Lion Protector, a military exercise involving members of the UK-led Joint Expeditionary Force (JEF).
The Faroe Islands, a self-governing part of the Kingdom of Denmark, lie between Scotland, Iceland and Norway and sit within the strategically important Greenland-Iceland-UK (GIUK) Gap.
The stretch of the North Atlantic has long been considered strategically important by Nato because vessels travelling between Russia's Arctic bases and the wider Atlantic can pass through the area.
READ MORE: UK Government addresses panic over diesel supplies as Donald Trump pressure grows
The Royal Navy said the latest deployment was intended to strengthen cooperation between JEF members and test their ability to respond rapidly to events in the region.
Royal Marines took part in exercises involving the boarding, searching and seizing of vessels, as well as small-boat missions and coastal landings across the Faroes' difficult terrain.
Commandos also established observation posts on clifftops to monitor maritime routes before carrying out cliff ascents.
General Sir Gwyn Jenkins, First Sea Lord and Commandant General Royal Marines, said: “Defending the Atlantic is fundamental to our economy, national security and way of life.
“In troubling times, we cannot be complacent.
“The return of the Royal Marines to the Faroe Islands should send an unequivocal message: the UK, alongside Denmark and our other allies in the Joint Expeditionary Force, stand ready to protect the waters, islands and vital routes that keep our nations secure.”
The deployment involved the UK Commando Force's Allied Reaction Force Special Operations Maritime Task Group (SOMTG).
The unit provides Nato with troops capable of deploying at short notice for operations including retaking vessels and offshore infrastructure and conducting coastal raids ahead of larger amphibious operations.
Exercise Lion Protector, which ran between August and October, was the task group's first major exercise.
It also marked the first time Royal Marines had been deployed to the Faroes since the Second World War.
British forces occupied the islands in April 1940 under Operation Valentine after Nazi Germany invaded Denmark.
READ MORE: Suella Braverman accused of being ‘racist against herself’ in Question Time clash
The move was intended to prevent Germany from taking control of the strategically located islands, which sit around 200 miles north-west of Scotland.
The Royal Navy initially sent two destroyers to the Faroese capital Tórshavn before around 250 Royal Marines landed from HMS Suffolk.
British forces remained on the islands until the end of the war in 1945, when control was returned to Denmark.
The new deployment comes amid an increased focus on security in the Arctic and North Atlantic as tensions with Russia continue to rise.
Exercise Lion Protector involved military activity across the High North and through the Danish Straits towards the Baltic Sea, with the JEF saying it was designed to rehearse potential responses to security threats in the region.

Smoke and fire was seen emerging from a site near the Aramco oil refinery in Riyadh, Saudi Arabia on Saturday, a witness told Reuters.
Pictures show plumes of dark smoke from the biggest refinery in the city. There was no immediate confirmation from Saudi authorities and Aramco did not immediately respond to a request for comment.
The fire comes amid escalating hostilities between Saudi Arabia and Yemen's Houthis, who have stepped up attacks on Saudi cities and energy infrastructure. Last week, the Houthis said they had attacked Saudi’s Aramco facilities in Yanbu with missiles and drones.
It comes as a crude oil tanker was reportedly struck by an unknown projectile off the coast of Oman, near the Strait of Hormuz, the UKMTO said on Saturday. All crew were reported safe and no environmental impact was recorded.
On Friday the UKMTO said a tanker was struck by a projectile while transiting the waterway, causing a small fire, which was extinguished.
Axios reported on Saturday that members of Donald Trump’s administration met in secret at Camp David to discuss the next steps of the war and the conflict between the Houthi rebels and Saudi Arabia.
Yemeni forces claim 97 'precision' attacks against Houthis
Yemeni government-aligned forces claim they conducted 97 “precision targeting operations” against the Houthis using aircraft, drones, artillery, missiles and snipers.
The attacks led to “neutralising (260) elements of the militia”, Yemeni military spokesperson Brigadier General Majid Abdullah Al-Nuzaili said in a post on X.
Earlier in the day, the Houthi military said it launched coordinated attacks targeting a Saudi Aramco facility in Riyadh in retaliation for recent Saudi coalition airstrikes against Sanaa and other Yemeni provinces.
Portuguese investigate US military access to base during Iran conflict
Portuguese prosecutors have opened a formal inquiry into the government's decision to allow US military flights to use Lajes Air Base in the Azores during the ongoing conflict with Iran.
The prosecutor general's office confirmed the probe following a legal complaint filed by the opposition Left Bloc party, which claims allowing US transit operations violates international law.
Under a 1951 bilateral treaty, Washington can utilise the strategic Atlantic hub freely during peacetime, but must secure explicit Portuguese approval once active hostilities begin.
Foreign minister Paulo Rangel defended the authorisation, stating Lisbon received firm assurances from Washington that US operations would remain defensive, necessary, and proportionate.
Unlike neighboring Spain, which restricted US access, Portugal's approval has ignited fierce political debate over the nation's indirect involvement in the conflict.
Iranian rial plunges to record low despite $2B central bank intervention
Iran’s rial has plummeted to a historic low, with the US dollar now trading above 2.68 million rials in spite of emergency central bank intervention.
State banks began selling up to $2 billion in foreign reserves to stabilise the currency, which has lost more than half its value over the past year.
However, severe sanctions and a naval blockade on Iranian oil exports continue to choke off the regime's primary source of foreign revenue, pushing domestic inflation past 70 percent.
Central bank officials dismissed the market crash as a temporary panic, accusing Washington of spreading false economic predictions to induce capital flight.
Two Iranian nationals charged over Manchester synagogue chlorine bomb plot
Two Iranian men appeared at Westminster Magistrates' Court on Saturday accused of planning a chemical bomb attack on Jewish targets in Manchester, including a synagogue targeted in a fatal attack last year.
Salam Ahmadyan, 36, and Rahman Salehi, 34, conducted "hostile reconnaissance" at Heaton Park Synagogue and the Manchester Jewish Museum, according to prosecutors.
The court heard the men were allegedly directed by a handler in Iran who provided instructions on building an improvised explosive device using household chemicals and brake fluid.
The alleged plot directly targeted the Heaton Park Synagogue on the anniversary of the October 2025 Yom Kippur attack, in which a gunman killed two worshipers before being shot dead by police.
Both suspects were remanded in custody ahead of an October 23 hearing at the Old Bailey.
Houthis claim missile and drone attack on Aramco facility in Riyadh
Yemen's Houthi rebels have claimed responsibility for a coordinated missile and drone strike targeting a Saudi Aramco facility in the capital city of Riyadh.
Witnesses reported seeing a large plume of smoke and fire rising near an Aramco installation in Riyadh earlier in the day.
The Houthi military has stated the assault was launched in direct retaliation for recent Saudi coalition airstrikes against Sanaa and other Yemeni provinces.
The reported strike marks a sharp escalation in cross-border targeting following claims last week of Houthi strikes against Aramco assets in Yanbu.
Iraq ships 2M barrels of crude through Strait of Hormuz
Iraq’s state-owned oil tanker company has transported two million barrels of crude oil through the Strait of Hormuz, marking its first such independent transit in decades.
Director general Ali Qais Abdul Jabbar confirmed on Saturday that the shipment shifts operations from delivering crude at the port of Basra to transporting it directly past the strategic chokepoint.
The move gives state oil marketer SOMO greater flexibility to secure better sales and pricing terms in international markets.
Abdul Jabbar added that the company is actively working to purchase specialised crude tankers to expand its state fleet and compete with regional maritime shipping firms.

Trump's top national security aides meet secretly at Camp David on Iran, Yemen, Axios reports
Donald Trump's top cabinet members met secretly at the presidential retreat at Camp David to discuss next steps in the Iran war and the Saudi-Houthi conflict in Yemen, Axios reported on Friday.

Beyond the Strait of Hormuz: How Gulf countries are preparing for life without the waterway
Port operator DP World is in talks to develop new facilities in the coastal area of Fujairah to take pressure off its flagship Jebel Ali port, according to the Financial Times.
Jebel Ali, built in 1977, has made the UAE a hub of finance and trade, but weeks ago it was set alight by a piece of fallen debris from an Iranian missile. Since then, Dubai International Airport, US military bases and other facilities have come under direct attack.
Colossal losses are no surprise considering that a huge 20 per cent of global oil supply all passes through the strategic waterway, which has remained deadlocked now for months.
With an interim agreement that was thinly constructed now falling apart by the day, it appears that Gulf countries are hatching plans to protect their own economies.
Trump sending 9,000 more troops to Middle East after threatening new strikes on Iran
The U.S. military is sending roughly 9,000 more troops to the Middle East aboard a group of ships, a U.S. official confirmed Thursday.
The bolstering of the American military presence comes as President Donald Trump warned that new strikes against Iran could be on the horizon.
The troop deployment, which includes a third aircraft carrier, underscores the rapidly evolving dynamic of Trump's war against Iran as he considers his next move, with midterm elections in the United States looming large and fresh signs that the nature of the conflict may be becoming more complex.

A team investigating a boat-shaped formation in eastern Turkey says new evidence is strengthening its case that the site could hold the remains of Noah's Ark.
"In archaeology, you deal with probabilities, and we're inching towards where we believe we will have confirmation this winter after our soil analysis is done with Sivas University, who's our partner in this," Noah's Ark Scans founder Andrew Jones told "Saturday in America."
The focus of the investigation is the Durupınar formation, an approximately 538-foot-long geological structure near Mount Ararat. Its shape and proximity to the region identified in the biblical account have fascinated Ark hunters for decades.
The boat-shaped formation was first discovered in 1959 and has long-drawn speculation over a possible connection to Noah's Ark.
Critics have maintained that the formation is naturally occurring, but Jones said recent drilling, soil sampling and ground-penetrating radar have given his team new reasons to challenge that conclusion.
"They've criticized in the past, saying all those scans you can interpret different ways, 'This is a solid mass of rock, a syncline or a block of bedrock,'" Jones said. "Well, we've core drilled… over 12 locations. We did not find bedrock at all."
Jones said the drilling uncovered rich black soil, which researchers plan to test for organic content this winter at Ankara University.
"Noah's Ark was a giant wooden boat, according to the Bible," he said.
"As wood decays, you're gonna find elevated organic matter. This year, as we drilled into the formation, we did not find a solid rock layer, like the critics said. But we did find large deposits of highly rich black soil that has hopefully high organics."
The researchers hope the analysis will help determine whether there are signs of human activity or materials consistent with decayed wood beneath the formation.
Jones also pointed to a 2024 soil survey that he said contained three times more organic matter inside the boat-shaped formation than samples collected just outside it.
Fox News' Andrea Margolis contributed to this report.

South Korean President Lee Jae Myung has accused Ukraine of attempting to provoke a war on the Korean Peninsula amid an escalating diplomatic dispute over Kiev’s public disclosure of the transfer of two North Korean prisoners of war to South Korea. Lee warned that Seoul would take “additional measures” against Ukraine unless it acknowledges what South Korea says was an agreement to keep the transfer confidential and issue a public apology. The dispute began after Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky publicly announced on September 23 that two North Korean soldiers captured during fighting in Russia’s Kursk Region had been transferred to South Korea, which has widely been criticised as illegal and contrary to their rights of repatriation as prisoners of war.
Lee has objected particularly strongly to Ukrainian comments concerning a potential military confrontation between North and South Korea. In a statement published on October 2, the South Korean president said he expressed “grave regret” that, rather than acknowledging the alleged agreement and apologising, Ukrainian officials were discussing an imminent military clash between the two Koreas. Lee described this as “attempting to provoke a war on the Korean Peninsula.” Ukraine could benefit considerably from a new war in Korea, as it would limit North Korea’s ability to divert supplies and personnel to support the Russian-led war effort in Eastern Europe. North Korea has been by far Russia’s most significant military supporter in the conflict.
The two North Korean personnel were captured by Ukrainian forces in January 2025 while serving alongside Russian forces. The two prisoners have particular significance because they are the first North Korean soldiers known to have been captured alive while participating in Russia’s war against Ukraine. Their delivery to South Korea could provide Seoul with information concerning North Korean military personnel, training and battlefield experience acquired during their deployment to Russia. South Korea has for over four years under three administrations consistently resisted Western pressure to send armaments to Ukraine, contrasting with the positions taken by other Western-aligned states.

Japan’s coast guard, citing the defence ministry, said the object may have been a ballistic missile and appeared to have come down, warning ships to take precautions.

Pyongyang’s Kim Yo-jong, the powerful sister of ruler Kim Jong-un, issued a statement on Friday that dismissed Seoul’s demand for an apology for what it said were North Korean mines that seriously wounded South Korean soldiers in the demilitarised zone – the heavily guarded buffer between the two Koreas.

According to Al Jazeera, Alon made the remarks during a Washington Institute for Near East Policy webcast on October 2, arguing that Israel could have reached the position it ultimately achieved “much earlier, maybe a year earlier or so”. He said the prolonged war may have cost the lives of hostages who could otherwise have been brought home alive.
Alon, who served as the Israeli military's point person for hostage negotiations during the war, said Israel's insistence on achieving “total victory” over Hamas before accepting a comprehensive deal was based on a false premise.
He argued that the October 2025 ceasefire and hostage agreement demonstrated that Israel could have achieved its broader strategic objectives while reaching a deal much earlier.
Alon said the decision to continue the war also had a human cost, arguing that an earlier agreement could have brought some hostages home alive and potentially saved thousands of lives on both sides.
He said Israel “could have and should have” shortened the war and returned the hostages earlier.
The October 2025 ceasefire agreement between Israel and Hamas came into effect on October 10, 2025, under a US-backed plan aimed at ending the Gaza war and securing the release of the remaining Israeli hostages.
Under the first phase of the deal, Hamas agreed to release all 20 living Israeli hostages, while Israel agreed to release Palestinian prisoners and detainees and withdraw its forces to agreed positions in Gaza.
The October 2025 deal came nearly two years after the October 7, 2023 Hamas-led attack on Israel, in which 251 people were abducted and taken to Gaza.
