A former Israeli general who was the army’s point person for hostage negotiations at the beginning of the Gaza war says that a deal to return all Israeli captives could have been achieved “much earlier” than October 2025 but it was prolonged unnecessarily.
“I think that we could [have gotten to] this point much earlier, maybe a year earlier or so, without any major implication on the other strategic goals of the war,” Major General Nitzan Alon said on Friday. “We missed it, actually. The war was too long.”
He was speaking during a Washington Institute for Near East Policy webcast marking three years since the October 7, 2023 Hamas attack on Israel preceding the genocidal war that has killed over 74,000 Palestinians.
Alon referred to Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s claim that Israel must achieve “total victory” before signing a deal as “false”.
He called the October 2025 “ceasefire” a “strategic achievement” that has since curbed Hamas’s military power. But he said it could have been secured much sooner with “maybe some hostages that got killed or murdered during their captivity [coming] back home alive.”
Hamas and Israel carried out a prisoner exchange deal in October 2025 under a ceasefire agreement that saw the release of nearly 2,000 Palestinians imprisoned in Israeli jails and 20 Israeli captives held in the Gaza Strip.
“We could have – and we should have – shortened the war, brought all the hostages back, maybe a year earlier, and moved forward and maybe, you know, saved thousands of lives on both sides,” Alon told the panel discussion organised by the United States think-tank.
Alon had made similar comments in July, when he also criticised Israeli Finance Minister Bezalel Smotrich, saying Smotrich had opposed some of the agreements put forward at various stages and therefore could not take credit for the return of all the captives.
‘Not just a missed opportunity, it’s tragic’
Speaking to Al Jazeera on Friday, former Israeli diplomat Alan Pinkas said Netanyahu had stalled the end of the war.
“A deal was possible very soon after the Hamas attack in October 2023,” he said.
“It took almost two years before the hostages were returned, so it’s not just a missed opportunity, it’s tragic.”
Earlier this week, Qatari Prime Minister Sheikh Mohammed bin Abdulrahman bin Jassim Al Thani said Israeli officials “rejected to entertain the idea” of a Hamas proposal to release all captives in exchange for a limited ceasefire soon after the attacks.
Al-Thani said Doha reached out to Israeli officials “on day one … Our message was very clear. They [Hamas leaders] are asking for a window of ceasefire to get the civilians out,” Sheikh Mohammed said in an interview with Piers Morgan. “And basically, they [the Israelis] were not interested to engage in the idea.”
Alon’s latest comments come less than a month before Israel’s October 27 legislative election, with polls showing the political battle remains at knife-edge.
Pinkas said Alon’s comments were unlikely to influence the outcome of the vote as polls already “reflect public anger” over the Netanyahu government’s failure to prevent the Hamas attacks.
A report by Israeli newspaper Haaretz claiming that United Arab Emirates President Sheikh Mohamed bin Zayed Al Nahyan had warned Netanyahu about a possible attack also sparked outrage across Israel last month.
Netanyahu said he would sue the outlet over its report, which he described as “fabricated” and “false”.

articles.title: Here's How Russia Plans to Pay for the Ukraine War in 2027 - themoscowtimes.com
articles.summary: Here's How Russia Plans to Pay for the Ukraine War in 2027  themoscowtimes.comSee more headlines & perspectives on Google News
articles.full_text:
Russia plans to raise defense spending to a post-Soviet high next year while cutting civilian programs and increasing taxes, signaling that the Kremlin is bracing for a prolonged war in Ukraine despite saying it is ready for peace talks.
The draft 2027 budget unveiled Thursday allocates 17.1 trillion rubles ($205.2 billion) to defense, 26% more than was earmarked for that year in the previous budget and 375% above the pre-war level of 2021.
Defense would account for roughly a third of federal spending next year, setting a post-Soviet record in nominal ruble terms.
Analysts say that Russia still has the resources to keep fighting, but that households, businesses and public services will bear more of the cost.
Economist Boris Grozovsky said Russia’s wartime economy still has a “considerable” financial cushion.
“But the message is clear: everyone will pay for the war, as much as they can. Wherever a little more money appears, the government will come for it, while handing out as little as possible itself,” he wrote in an analysis published by the exiled outlet IStories.
The published defense allocation does not capture the full cost of the war. Russia has released only planned military spending rather than actual outlays since 2022, while classified budget items make the overall bill difficult to establish.
Soaring war costs have put increasing pressure on state finances. The federal budget deficit reached 5.65 trillion rubles ($67.8 billion), or 2.6% of gross domestic product, in 2025.
The government projects a shortfall of 7.3 trillion rubles ($87.6 billion), or 3.2% of GDP, for 2026 before it narrows to 5.4 trillion rubles ($64.8 billion), or 2.2%, in 2027.
In a forecast published before the draft budget was unveiled, economists at Russia’s largest lender Sberbank put next year’s deficit at 2.7% of GDP, questioning whether the government could deliver the spending restraint and higher non-oil and gas revenues needed to meet its earlier target.
This deficit is high by recent Russian standards, but it is still manageable and remains lower than in many European countries, such as France (5.4% of GDP) and Britain (4.3% of GDP).
The projected deficit does not in itself point to an imminent fiscal crisis, but containing it while increasing military spending is becoming more difficult.
The government plans to borrow 6.1 trillion rubles ($73.2 billion) next year, up from 5 trillion rubles ($60 billion) in 2026, to help finance the deficit.
Yet debt servicing is projected to reach 4.6 trillion rubles ($55.2 billion) in 2027, or 9.4% of total federal spending. Those costs remain high because the Central Bank has kept interest rates elevated to contain stubborn inflation that has been fueled by heavy government spending.
To help close the gap, Moscow is also cutting civilian spending and planning another round of tax increases for a third consecutive year.
The draft reduces allocations for healthcare by 5.5%, education by 5.4% and social programs by 6% compared with the amounts previously budgeted for 2027.
Some of Russia's national projects, government programs targeting priorities like healthcare and infrastructure, will also face cuts going forward.
Funding for the Long and Active Life project, which supports health initiatives, would fall by about 20%, from 181.1 billion rubles ($2.17 billion) in 2026 to 145.9 billion rubles ($1.75 billion) next year.
The allocation for the federal cancer program would drop from 44.9 billion rubles ($538.8 million) to 3.9 billion rubles ($46.8 million).
The proposed tax measures are expected to raise an additional 1.5 trillion rubles ($18 billion).
They include a 22% value-added tax on purchases from foreign online retailers and a customs fee of 100 rubles, or about $1.20, on each parcel worth less than 200 euros.
Tax rates on income from sources including deposit interest, dividends and property sales would rise from a range of 13% to 15% to a range of 13% to 22%. The Finance Ministry has also proposed a one-time windfall tax on mining and metals companies.
The changes to taxes on passive income are expected to raise the most revenue, up to 700 billion rubles ($8.4 billion), followed by levies on online purchases, which would bring in another 500 billion rubles ($6 billion).
Analyst Alexandra Prokopenko said the budget showed defense spending growing faster than overall expenditure, squeezing the funds available for other purposes.
In an analysis for Carnegie Politika, she warned that the government may soon be approaching the limits of how much additional revenue it can raise through taxes to fund the war.
That could increase pressure on the Central Bank to support the wartime economy by cutting interest rates to reduce borrowing costs for the government and businesses, as well as increase debt restructuring for struggling companies, she said.

articles.title: A Shakshuka in the Gulf: U.S. Options in the Iran War - The Soufan Center
articles.summary: A Shakshuka in the Gulf: U.S. Options in the Iran War  The Soufan Center
articles.full_text:
INTELBRIEF
October 2, 2026
A Shakshuka in the Gulf: U.S. Options in the Iran War
In American slang, “in a stew” means to be in a difficult situation. Italians say pasticciaccio — a baked pasta dish — to describe an awful mess. Israelis prepare shakshuka, a delicious North African stew, but it can also mean a chaotic situation.
The current situation in the Gulf is a shakshuka — a complicated mess. It involves a host of adversaries operating on multiple fronts. The U.S. and Israel can turn up the heat, but that may cause the pot to boil over with consequences far beyond the region. This IntelBrief examines Washington’s options. Iranians and their proxies in Lebanon, Yemen, and Iraq have their own calculations.
In his recent speech to the UN General Assembly, U.S. President Donald Trump outlined a binary approach to the conflict: either a deal or annihilation. In reality, the situation is more complicated. There are no easy military solutions.
The U.S. can assemble a naval coalition to restore free passage through the Strait of Hormuz. Considerable progress has been made in keeping oil flowing through the Strait — crude oil is currently being shipped at 80 percent of the pre-war volume. Adding the amounts that are being pumped through pipelines, the total is reportedly at 98 percent of the pre-war volume. Far less refined products are being shipped, but that is because of the damage inflicted on infrastructure. And shipments of other vital products like fertilizers remain below pre-war volumes.
To guarantee the continued safety of merchant vessels and oil terminals would require continued naval escorts and protection of port facilities. The burden for this will fall largely on the United States. The Europeans have indicated their reluctance to send warships to the Gulf. It is difficult to envision a scenario where American allies would contribute to an air or a naval campaign in a war initiated without any consultation. The United States needs to end Iran’s ability to threaten shipping once and for all or at least dissuade Tehran from using it.
The U.S. can continue its naval blockade of Iranian ports. The blockade is just the physical manifestation of a broader sanctions regime. Taken together, the sanctions and blockade have been highly effective at cutting off trade. The Iranian economy has been devastated. The U.S. believes that the combination of sanctions and blockade will force Iran’s leadership to yield.
It remains difficult, however, to assess Iran’s tolerance for pain. Siege warfare is slow, naval deployments are costly, and Iran’s leaders themselves will be the last to suffer. The U.S. had Iraq under economic siege for years. It brought about economic collapse and a humanitarian crisis, but it still took an invasion to bring down Saddam Hussein.
And it is difficult to maintain a siege when it causes continuing damage to the world economy. The U.S. can increase economic pressure. With “Operation Economic Outcast,” announced by Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent in August 2026, the U.S. has expanded its sanctions to include secondary sanctions. Whatever other options the U.S. may consider, it will no doubt continue its campaign to keep shipping lanes open while it tightens the economic screws. It could also escalate the conflict in a variety of ways, as President Trump threatened in his UN address.
The United States can increase its targeted killings of Iranian leadership. The U.S. killed hundreds of al-Qaeda and Islamic State (ISIS) leaders and cadre during the Global War on Terrorism (as well as Qasem Soleimani, the commander of Iran’s Quds Force). These efforts degraded the groups’ command and control capabilities, but they continued to operate. It is not clear that killing another layer of Iranian leaders would significantly change the situation, unless the killings were sustained. Some have argued that the killing of Iran’s top leaders at the outset of the war in February ushered in an even less compromising leadership. We will return to this point at the end.
The United States could initiate a joint U.S. and Saudi campaign in Yemen. Saudi Arabia requested substantial U.S. military support for operations against the Houthi rebels who now control most of the coast along the straits into the Red Sea. Despite the risk of alienating an important ally that has provided military support to American efforts against Iran, the U.S. rejected the Saudi request.
U.S. rejection may reflect America’s assessment of the situation. The Saudis have been militarily involved in Yemen’s civil war since 2015 and have not managed to quell the Houthi rebellion, which has continued to gain strength. The Yemeni government forces have repeatedly proved ineffectual. Moreover, U.S. intervention would not solve the Iranian issue or open the Strait of Hormuz, and American supplies of some critical munitions are reportedly low. (The UK has offered limited air refueling assistance to the Saudi campaign.)
As it did in the campaign against ISIS, the U.S. could attempt to assemble a coalition to conduct a continuing bombing campaign against Iran. This could target a broader array of infrastructure, although Iranian civilians will suffer most, and Iran, as it has already demonstrated, will find ways to retaliate against America’s Gulf partners. The American rejection of Saudi’s request for assistance in Yemen makes a coalition campaign less likely. It would most likely be a unilateral operation.
More ambitiously, as it did in the First Gulf War, the United States could try to assemble a U.S. air and ground coalition, perhaps including Kurdish and other forces aimed at seizing enough territory in Iran to re-open the Strait of Hormuz. The problem is that it will take months to assemble the force and put in place the logistics basing necessary to support the operation; it cannot be done from Diego Garcia. It also cannot be done secretly, giving Iran time to put pressure, including military attacks, sabotage, and terrorist operations against countries hosting the supply depots. The United States did not seek to create a broad coalition before initiating hostilities, and most European governments will not join.
The United States learned a great deal about supporting proxy forces in Afghanistan, Iraq, and Syria. It could increase support for a Kurdish force to open a front in Iran’s north. The idea is not to support Kurdish separatism, but to create a sanctuary for fleeing Iranians. A U.S.-protected zone would facilitate the creation of an Iranian rebel force that can then advance on the ground with U.S. air support.
This could be done more quickly and less expensively than assembling a large expeditionary force. Iran has more than 90 million people, including many from various religious and ethnic identities oppressed by the government. Infantry soldiers can be trained in weeks. Higher-ranking Iranian officers can be incentivized to defect.
The operation’s success would depend on the willingness and ability of Iranians to join a resistance movement. In 2014, the U.S. was able to assemble and support a Kurdish effort against ISIS, but earlier U.S. efforts to support a secular rebel force to bring down Assad failed. The thought of fracturing Iran on behalf of an outside power could alienate many ethnic Persians who do not support the regime. And it could produce an adverse reaction. Iraq’s invasion of Iran in the 1980s galvanized Iranians.
And promises of sustained U.S. support may be heavily discounted. In 1991, the U.S. encouraged Kurdish and Shia rebellions after the Gulf War, but did not intervene when Saddam Hussein brutally crushed them, and after dismantling ISIS’s caliphate, the U.S. abandoned its Kurdish allies in Iraq and Syria.
A further danger with these more ambitious plans is that, faced with an existential threat, the Iranian regime can inflict terrible damage on the neighboring Gulf states by attacking desalination plants and oil and gas infrastructure. The United Arab Emirates (UAE) even operates nuclear power plants. Even now, there are probably diehards in the IRGC who are preparing, or have already prepared, Götterdämmerung scenarios.
Annihilation. In his recent address to the United Nations General Assembly, President Trump has tabled his own stark choice: “Will a deal be made with Iran that lets them rebuild a far greater country than it ever was before … Or do I annihilate the Islamic Republic … drive them into hell with no chance of survival and no hope of future greatness or generations?”
While the rhetoric is threatening, the Gulf states Washington would depend on to expand its military operations against the Islamic Republic might read the President’s message differently. They could interpret the ambiguity as signaling an equal readiness to cut a deal, leaving them exposed to greater danger as U.S. partners. Just hours after his speech, President Trump told reporters that U.S. officials had a “very good” three-hour meeting with Iranian leaders.
There are other indicators: In September, the State Department shifted $52 million in foreign military assistance from the Middle East to Latin America. The sum is not great, but it indicates a shift in strategic priorities as the U.S. ramps up its determination to take down Latin America’s drug cartels. As much as America’s Gulf partners may despise Iran, they could calculate that the lesser of two evils is to cut their own deals first with Iran.
The United States has not stuck to a consistent message about its goals for this war. That makes it difficult to evaluate alternate strategies. Each option entails costs and comes with unpredictable consequences. The difficulty the U.S. faces in Iran is translating the powerful military blows it has inflicted on Iran into a lasting political outcome. Absent a clear idea of where the goal posts are makes it even harder to measure the benefits.

articles.summary: European powers answer Russian nuclear warnings with further military escalation  wsws.org
articles.full_text:
Barely days after Moscow formally warned NATO that an attempt to blockade or isolate the Russian enclave of Kaliningrad could provoke the use of nuclear weapons, the governments of Europe are responding not with attempts to step back from the brink, but with declarations of increased military support for Ukraine, accelerated rearmament and preparations for a direct confrontation with Russia.
The public posture of the European governments is one of extraordinary brinkmanship. Each Russian warning is dismissed as intimidation or bluff, while each new confrontation is invoked as the justification for still greater military escalation.
On Thursday, German Chancellor Friedrich Merz appeared in Münster alongside Dutch Prime Minister Rob Jetten and NATO Secretary General Mark Rutte at the headquarters of the 1st German-Netherlands Corps.
Merz declared that the Ukraine war “concerns us very directly,” pledged that Germany and its allies would support Kiev “with all our strength,” and said Berlin was working “at full speed” to ensure the credible military deterrence of Russia. He explicitly connected this policy to increased investment in Germany’s “military strength” and “economic resilience.”
Jetten declared that Europe confronted a “new security reality” and had to demonstrate that it was prepared to do “whatever it takes” to defend itself. He pointed to rising military expenditure, F-35 deployments, accelerated joint arms production and German-Dutch intelligence cooperation that has been raised to an “unprecedented level.”
Rutte was even more explicit. Russia, he said, was attempting to frighten NATO into reducing its support for Ukraine. His answer was to “keep calm, carry on, and continue the support for Ukraine.” He added that NATO’s response to Russian actions would be to provide still more support to Ukraine.
The setting underscored the military significance of these declarations. According to NATO, the German-Netherlands Corps is a “warfighting headquarters” capable of commanding an international force of 50,000 troops and is responsible for NATO forces assigned to the defence of Estonia and Latvia on Russia’s Baltic frontier. The meeting took place immediately before Rutte received the “International Award of the Peace of Westphalia” on behalf of NATO.
These statements come directly after Russia sent NATO a diplomatic note warning that it was prepared to employ “the entire arsenal of forces and capabilities at its disposal, including nuclear weapons” if NATO attempted to isolate Kaliningrad. The document also referred to the possibility of Russian strikes against “decision-making centers” in NATO countries from the outset of such a conflict. Kaliningrad, situated between Poland and Lithuania, is one of Russia’s most heavily militarised regions.
At the same time, Lithuania is advancing a constitutional amendment that would abolish Article 137, which prohibits weapons of mass destruction and foreign military bases on Lithuanian territory. On September 22, the Lithuanian parliament voted 99 to 13, with five abstentions, to advance the amendment. Further votes are required before the constitutional change can take effect. Its adoption would remove the existing constitutional obstacle to the future stationing of nuclear weapons in a NATO state directly bordering Kaliningrad and Belarus.
The Kremlin responded Thursday. Spokesman Dmitry Peskov warned governments contemplating the stationing of nuclear weapons close to Russia that they were “deeply mistaken” if they believed this would increase their security. Such moves, he said, would instead produce “further escalation and increased tensions.” Referring to European participation in the Ukraine war, Peskov added: “If you take part in a war on someone’s side, you cannot avoid consequences of various kinds.”
Putin personally reinforced the warning later Thursday. Speaking at the Valdai Discussion Club in Moscow, he declared that a direct attack on Russian territory, specifically including Kaliningrad, would place the use of “all the weapons at our country’s disposal” “inevitably and immediately” on the agenda.
He then issued an extraordinary warning about the dynamics of the confrontation itself. “The logic of escalating, increasingly harsh retaliatory measures leads to a fatal point of no return,” Putin said. He warned that this point could arrive “very quickly and unexpectedly” and referred explicitly to arsenals capable of destroying “all life” or reducing the planet to a catastrophic state.
These threats by the Kremlin offer no progressive alternative to NATO’s escalation. The Putin regime speaks for the Russian capitalist oligarchy. Its answer to imperialist encirclement and military pressure is Russian nationalism, military retaliation and nuclear threats—a reactionary strategy that itself pushes the world further toward catastrophe.
But it would be politically criminal to dismiss Moscow’s warnings on this account.
The European powers are operating on the assumption that Russia can be subjected indefinitely to deep strikes, economic warfare, expanding NATO deployments and preparations around its internationally recognised territory without eventually responding directly against the states organising and enabling this campaign.
No government can know where the limit lies.
The danger arises precisely because every previous threshold crossed without a Russian response encourages the conclusion that the next one can also be crossed. Ukrainian attacks on Moscow become normalised. Strikes on Russian refineries and strategic military installations become normalised. NATO exercises demonstrating the capacity to isolate Kaliningrad become normalised. The removal of constitutional restrictions on nuclear deployments becomes normalised.
Putin’s own warning about the “logic of escalating, increasingly harsh retaliatory measures” underscores the danger. Once the credibility of nuclear and conventional deterrence becomes bound up with demonstrating a willingness to retaliate, each side’s actions become the justification for the next escalation, and the confrontation assumes an increasingly uncontrollable logic.
The contrast within the European political establishment could hardly be clearer. Bulgarian Prime Minister Rumen Radev warned Wednesday that “no one is raising the question about nuclear risk” and asked whether Europe had even seriously assessed the consequences of attempting “a conventional victory over the biggest nuclear power.” He rejected Moscow’s nuclear rhetoric but called for diplomatic channels to be reopened.
Rutte responded that he did not take the Russian warning seriously because Putin “can never win against NATO.” EU Defence Commissioner Andrius Kubilius rejected calls for renewed diplomacy and insisted instead that Putin must “feel that war is coming to Russia itself.”
The issue, therefore, is not that the danger has gone unnoticed. Dominant sections of the European ruling class have concluded that retreat is politically and strategically unacceptable and seek further escalation.
As was the case with the world wars of the twentieth century, this recklessness has an objective basis.
The First World War arose fundamentally from irreconcilable conflicts between the imperialist powers over markets, colonies and the division of the world. But the ruling classes also entered the war amid enormous domestic tensions and a growing socialist workers’ movement.
War then provided the framework for suppressing class conflict under the banner of national unity. In Germany, the Burgfrieden suspended political conflicts, and the SPD voted for the war credits on August 4, 1914. Shortly before this historic betrayal, the SPD had still organised mass anti-war protests involving roughly three-quarters of a million people.
There is an analogous relationship today between external military escalation and internal social crisis, although under vastly different historical conditions.
Nowhere is this clearer than in France. Tuesday’s public-sector strike brought hundreds of thousands onto the streets against wage freezes, austerity and the deterioration of public services. At the same time, an explosive movement among high-school students has spread across the country. By Wednesday, protests and blockades had affected 356 high schools, while more than 2,000 people—most of them minors—had been arrested over two days. Students have protested teacher shortages, overcrowded classrooms, dilapidated school buildings and intolerable learning conditions.
On Thursday, university students began joining the movement. Around 30 university campuses were reported blocked, including in Paris, Strasbourg, Marseille, Lyon, Reims, Poitiers and Nanterre. Prime Minister Sébastien Lecornu convened an interministerial crisis meeting and ordered ministers to cancel official travel as the unrest continued to spread.
The developments inevitably evoke the experience of May 1968. Then, a student revolt became the detonator for the intervention of millions of workers and the largest general strike in French history. Today, once again, anger among youth is developing alongside increasingly bitter struggles by workers against austerity and the destruction of public services.
The decisive question is how and when broader sections of the working class intervene independently.
This is precisely what the ruling classes throughout Europe fear. Their governments confront economic stagnation, industrial decline, exploding military budgets, attacks on pensions and public services, mounting political instability and profound popular hostility to the existing parties. War does not originate simply as a device for diverting attention from these problems. It arises from the same crisis of the capitalist system and inter-imperialist antagonisms that produce the social crisis at home.

articles.summary: Yemen’s army says targets Houthis in hundreds of strikes, killing 700  Al JazeeraFighting Intensifies in Yemen, Raising Fresh Fears of All-Out War  The New York TimesYemen's armed forces say it is conducting strikes against Houthis in Sanaa  reuters.comSaudi Arabia launched more than 90 attacks in Yemen in 24 hours, Houthis claim - report  The Jerusalem PostHouthis say Saudi Arabia launched dozens of strikes on Yemen capital  The Times of Israel
articles.full_text:
The Yemeni army says it has carried out hundreds of strikes on the capital, Sanaa, and other areas held by the Iran-backed Houthis, as the battle for control of the country’s most populated regions intensifies.
Colonel Majed Abdullah al-Nazili, the spokesman for Yemen’s internationally recognised government forces, said on Saturday that the military “executed 257 precision targeting operations” against Houthi sites, movements, and military capabilities.
The army used “warplanes, drones, artillery, missiles, and rocket launchers”, he added in a post on X.
Al-Nazili said initial estimates indicate the operations killed at least 700 Houthi rebels and destroyed “strategic and high-value military targets”, including 170 combat vehicles and heavy equipment.
The army spokesman did not mention any casualties among government forces.
The strikes “had a direct impact on the [Houthi] militia’s combat capability and limited its ability to continue its attacks against civilians in their homes and villages”, he said.
Saturday’s operations targeted Sanaa, Midi, Baqim, and the front lines in al-Jawf, Marib, al-Bayda, and Lahij, with the heaviest operational efforts concentrated around Taiz, al-Nazili added.
On Friday, al-Nazili said Yemen’s government forces had carried out nearly 500 military operations, killing or wounding 1,540 Houthi rebels in 24 hours.
Taiz focal point of clashes
The government-held city of Taiz has become a focal point of the renewed fighting.
Al Jazeera’s Maha Ali, reporting from Taiz on Saturday, said the region is seeing continued escalation and intense fighting across several fronts around the city, with some of the fiercest fighting happening on its western outskirts.
The Houthis have used an exceptionally heavy volume of fire during the assault, she noted, adding that the sound of continuing artillery fire, particularly from the Houthi side targeting western areas, could still be heard.
Residents are appealing for evacuation as the shelling continues, Ali reported, adding that there have been civilian casualties in the fighting, including from a shell that hit a residential area in Dhubab, killing a baby who died from shrapnel injuries.
On the Samaa front, she said, the Houthis made advances on Friday in the mountainous area, and fierce clashes are continuing there between government forces and the rebels. Several field sources told Ali that large numbers of residents have left Samaa, something, she said, that had not happened on this scale in more than a decade.
Following those clashes, Yemeni government forces took control of the Samaa fort, southeast of the city of Taiz, after heavy fighting, the government-run Saba news agency reported.
A military source told Saba that the armed forces, backed by local popular resistance fighters from the Samaa district, secured the fort after “violent battles”, leaving dozens of Houthi fighters killed or wounded while others fled.
Key border crossing closed
On Saturday, the army’s media official Ammar al-Sami’i told Al Jazeera that the government had closed the al-Houban crossing in Taiz.
The crossing had previously been closed for nine years and was later reopened to civilians in 2024 for “humanitarian reasons”, Sami’i said, as the road is one of Yemen’s most important connections between territory held by the opposing sides. It connects Houthi-held al-Houban to government-held Taiz city.
Sami’i said security reasons are behind the closure, following an attempt by the Houthis to infiltrate Taiz via the road, attacks in the vicinity and a general military build-up.
A fragile truce struck between the government and the Houthis in 2022 collapsed in July this year, and fighting in Yemen has escalated significantly since then.
In mid-September, the Houthis swept across parts of western Yemen, seizing the port city of Mocha and key strategic islands in the Bab al-Mandeb strait.
Since then, anti-Houthi forces have largely stabilised the front lines.
Hundreds of thousands of people have been displaced since the fighting restarted.
Yemen has been embroiled in civil war since the Houthis seized the capital of Sanaa in 2014, forcing the internationally recognised government to retreat to Aden.

articles.title: 'Anger in the streets': Tens of thousands protest in Spain over housing crisis - BBC
articles.summary: 'Anger in the streets': Tens of thousands protest in Spain over housing crisis  BBCSpanish Lawmakers Reject Eviction Freeze, Spurring Calls for Early Elections  The New York TimesSpain: Massive protests after housing bills voted down  dw.comSpain’s housing crisis is a warning for all of Europe – rights mean nothing if they’re not enforced  The ConversationThe right and wrong lessons to learn from Spain’s housing crisis  ft.com
articles.full_text:
Tens of thousands of people have protested across Spain calling for greater protections for tenants after the government failed to pass emergency housing legislation.
About 50 marches took place on Saturday in cities including Madrid, Valencia and Barcelona.
"There is a lot of anger in the streets," a spokesperson for the Valencia Tenants' Union said. Clashes have taken place between some protesters and police in the city.
The measures put forward by Pedro Sánchez's leftist coalition government on Friday followed public outcry over the eviction of an 87-year-old woman from her home last month after she was unable to afford a sharp rent increase.
Her eviction triggered nationwide protests across Spain with protesters demanding lower rents, an end to evictions, and a ban on investment funds - or "vulture funds" as the government has termed them - buying property.
Sanchez's defeat in Congress on Friday heightens speculation that he might call an early general election, which was not due until next summer.
His coalition government, made up of his ruling Socialist party and junior partner the Sumar alliance, does not command a majority in parliament.
Photographs showed protesters in the east coast city of Valencia clashing with police officers on Saturday near arts centre Palau de les Arts Reina Sofía, which was hosting a real estate summit.
Several protesters removed barriers and threw objects at officers, who responded with rubber bullets, Spanish media reported. Public broadcaster RTVE said nine police officers were injured and five people were arrested.
One of the biggest demonstration happened in the capital, Madrid, where estimates of the number of participants varied widely. The city's Tenants' Union said there were 500,000, while officials put the figure at 70,000.
Demonstrators held banners reading "There won't be peace for rentism" and "I study to have a future, not to have a tiny apartment". They shook the keys they were holding and chanted: "We have the keys of all the city".
Some had also camped in one of the city's main squares, Puerta del Sol, for days.
One protester, David, told RTVE ahead of the protest: "We're not here for pleasure or comfort. We're here out of conviction."
Another protester, 26-year-old librarian Marcos Sainz, told AFP news agency that he used to share a two-bedroom flat with friends, paying 900 euros (£766) a month in rent. Today, he said a one-bedroom flat often costs 1,000 euros.
Sainz said he would protest against rent rises "until someone dares to regulate it all", or "we'll all have to leave Madrid".
Spanish police said they had arrested three members of a far-right group, some of whom had performed Nazi salutes, as they tried to reach demonstrators in the square.
On Friday night, Madrid's Tenants' Union said that although the government's proposed measures were insufficient, the rejection of the proposed legislation "exacerbates the housing crisis which is costing the working class their lives".
It is calling for a general strike over the housing crisis.
The legislation put forward in Congress on Friday was divided into two decrees.
The first included the suspension of evictions of vulnerable tenants until 2030, a two-year extension to rental leases due to expire before 2028, tax increases for tourist apartments, and a restriction on the purchase of residential properties by so-called "vulture funds".
The second decree included the automatic renewal of rental contracts, a major demand of many on the left and the Tenants' Union.
MPs rejected the first decree by 178 votes to 172 and voted against the second by 184 to 166.
Prior to the vote, the conservative People's Party (PP) and far-right Vox had already said they would vote against both initiatives, leaving the minority government depending on the support of smaller nationalist parties in Catalonia and the Basque Country.
However, by the eve of the parliamentary session, the centre-right, pro-independence Together for Catalonia (JxCat) had signalled its opposition to both laws, condemning them to failure.
Sánchez's ruling coalition hurriedly drew up the decree laws in an effort to defuse the housing protests that were sparked when 87-year-old Maricarmen Abascal was evicted in September.
The social backlash led to the company that owns Abascal's flat, Urbagestión, negotiating her return to the flat on a low rent. However, protests have continued.
The Bank of Spain estimates the country is short of 700,000 homes, based on the gap between demand and new construction.
House prices have risen by 12.2% in the past year, according to figures for the second quarter of 2026 from national statistics institute INE.
The shortage in rental housing means that costs rose by 8.5% in 2025, according to real estate firm Idealista, with Madrid alone seeing an increase of 9.7% in rents.
It said Barcelona and Madrid were Spain's most expensive cities to rent a home, at €23.80 per square metre and €22.70 per square metre respectively.

articles.summary: Moscow unveils 'new doctrine' targeting Ukrainian civilians, Zelensky vows to respond with more energy strikes  The Kyiv IndependentUkraine war briefing: Kyiv to increase oil refinery attacks because of Moscow’s winter strategy, Zelenskyy says  The GuardianEXCLUSIVE: Ukraine will hit Russian refineries in response to Moscow's 'new doctrine' of airstrikes, Zelenskiy says  ReutersPutin has told military leaders to abandon rules of war, Zelenskyy says  Financ...
articles.full_text:
In response to a new airstrike policy targeting Ukrainian civilians by Moscow, President Volodymyr Zelensky said on Oct. 3 that Ukraine would increase attacks on Russian energy infrastructure.
Zelensky told Reuters that Ukrainian intelligence obtained documents revealing that Russian President Vladimir Putin issued a "new doctrine" allowing Russian forces to launch broader strikes against Ukrainian civilian targets this upcoming winter.
"We saw documents and we know that they allow them [to] attack infrastructure ... logistics ... roads, schools, hospitals, to pressure people to leave the capital, leave different cities," Zelensky said. With this shift, Putin wants to appear strong even as Russian troops continue to lose ground while suffering massive casualties, said Zelensky.
The president's comments come as Russian forces have increasingly battered Ukrainian civilian infrastructure in recent weeks, including attacks on key bridges and medical and educational facilities.
In response to Moscow's changing tactics, Zelensky vowed to increase strikes on Russian energy sites, though without indiscriminately targeting Russian civilians.
"We have to respond in any way [we can]. With their attacks on our energy, we have to respond on their energy. First of all, oil refineries: what gives money to them for this war," Zelensky said. "But we will not respond, of course, just like them, on any civilian objects."
For weeks, U.S. President Donald Trump has been pressing Ukraine and Russia to halt energy strikes in order to help lower high oil prices brought on by his war with Iran. While Zelensky has expressed his willingness to try an energy ceasefire, the American president's pleas appear to have gained little traction in Moscow.
In order to help double down on striking Russian energy sites, Ukraine will continue to produce its own long-range ballistic missiles. On Oct. 1, Zelensky announced Ukraine's domestically developed FP-7 ballistic missile was used in combat against Russia for the first time.
Zelensky told Reuters he has already called on the missile's manufacturer, Fire Point, to prepare longer-range missiles.
"I said to them, where is my FP-9? We need the FP-9. And the FP-9 will be [ready] this autumn, I'm sure," Zelensky said.
On Oct. 3, Zelensky said Ukraine had responded to Russian strikes on civilian targets by using long-range missiles to hit a facility in Russia's Samara region as well as an "Iskander" missile systems in the Bryansk region.
"Russians continue to turn our infrastructure and everything that supports normal life into targets," said Zelensky. "It is important to note that our soldiers always find ways to respond justly to these attacks and to return the war to where it came from."

Ukraine will double down on attacking Russian oil refineries in response to a new policy of airstrikes by Moscow designed to force people to abandon Kyiv and other cities, but will not target civilians, President Volodymyr Zelensky said.
Ukrainian intelligence has obtained documents showing that Russian leader Vladimir Putin had issued a “new doctrine” of military attacks on a much broader range of civilian targets ahead of winter, Zelensky said.
“We saw documents and we know that they allow them to attack infrastructure ... logistics ... roads, schools, hospitals, to pressure people to leave the capital, leave different cities,” Zelensky said. “This is the goal of the operation.”
Driving the shift in policy, Zelensky said, was Putin's desire to appear strong at a time when his military was losing ground in a key frontline region and sustaining higher levels of casualties.
The Kremlin was not available to comment on Saturday. But in a statement urging foreign nationals to leave Kyiv, the Russian Foreign Ministry said Moscow would continue to systematically hit targets in what it said were retaliatory strikes for Ukrainian attacks on Russia in recent months.
Both sides deny deliberately targeting civilians.
Counteroffensive in Donbas
Zelensky said an ongoing Ukrainian counteroffensive, code-named “Vivaldi,” had recaptured around 140 sq km (54 sq miles) of Ukraine's eastern Donbas region, which Russia has said it must control in its entirety as a condition for any peace deal.
In recent weeks, U.S. President Donald Trump's administration has sought to revive talks to end the four-year-old conflict — Europe's bloodiest since World War Two.
The U.S. leader last month urged Ukraine to refrain from hitting Russian oil installations, saying that was sending global diesel prices surging.
But Zelensky, speaking as air raid sirens blared outside the gilded halls of the presidential offices, said he had received no indications from Russia that Putin was interested in peace talks or discussing a ceasefire on energy infrastructure.
Over the past week, the Ukrainian capital has come under persistent attack by Russian drones and missiles targeting energy and telecoms assets, road and rail infrastructure. For the first time, Russia has targeted the bridges across the Dnipro River connecting east and west Kyiv.
Zelensky said Ukraine would respond to the change in tactics by Moscow, but would not respond in kind by targeting civilian infrastructure indiscriminately.
“We have to respond in any way (we can). With their attacks on our energy, we have to respond on their energy. First of all, oil refiners: what gives money to them for this war,” Zelensky said in English. “But we will not respond, of course, just like them, on any civilian objects.”
Support from Europe
After the Trump administration invited Putin to attend a G20 summit in Miami in December and discussed business deals with Russian envoys, Zelensky urged Washington not to normalise relations with Russia before ensuring a return to peace.
Zelensky said he would be happy to meet Putin for peace talks at the G20, but he warned the U.S. not to believe in “illusions” that Russia would end hostilities if it gained control of Donbas.
“It's not fair just to normalize,” said Zelensky, dressed in his trademark black T-shirt and military-style jacket. Any resumption of economic and diplomatic ties with the West had to be in return for peace, he said: “Because peace is more important than any kind of economy.”
While the U.S. has proposed resuming trilateral talks in the coming weeks in the UAE, Zelensky noted that an exact date and location for the technical-level conversations had not been set.
Ukrainian officials warn that Russia has stockpiled hundreds of ballistic missiles ahead of an expected winter onslaught against electricity and water infrastructure. Last winter, the worst of the war, Russian strikes left swathes of the country without electricity and heating for days at a time.
Since the summer, Moscow has also begun launching dozens of fast and relatively cheap jet-powered Shahed drones a day at Ukraine, whose air defenses have struggled as its previous generation of interceptor drones are too slow to catch them.
Zelensky said Ukraine had been forced to rely heavily on its fighter aircraft — F-16s and MiGs — to down around 60% of the Russian jet-powered drones, but supplies of 20 mm ammunition for the planes were running low.
Kyiv was urgently working on other solutions — including boosting its jamming capabilities, he said. In the second half of October, it should receive its first shipment of small, cheap air defense missiles capable of hitting the new Shaheds.
Last week, Zelensky said Ukraine was developing five models of new interceptor drones capable of downing the jet Shaheds. Fresh from a meeting with his defense chiefs, he said tests on two of those models showed a modest success rate of around 30%.
“We'll have to scale it,” he said. “I hope that with all these things, with all these elements, we'll find a way.”
Ballistic threat
Ukraine announced the first combat use this week of its own domestically made ballistic missile — the FP-7, which has a range of around 250 km (155 miles).
Zelensky said he had called the manufacturer Fire Point to pressure executives to quickly finish a longer-range model, the FP-9, which the company has said could hit Moscow.
“I said to them, ‘Where is my FP-9?’” said Zelensky, with a grin. “We need the FP-9. And the FP-9 will be (ready) this autumn, I'm sure.”
Zelensky said a recent spate of Russian drone incursions and hybrid attacks in Europe were an effort to intimidate European populations and to divide support for Ukraine.
Some European leaders were starting to understand this, he said, and toughen their position.
Russia says such accusations are baseless and the result of anti-Russian hysteria.
After talks with European officials in Brussels this week, Ukraine found funding to proceed with orders for drones that it needs to keep fighting at the start of 2027, Zelensky said.
Ukrainian officials had worked on a plan with European partners to plug a $27 billion hole in Kyiv's defense budget this year.
The plans involve a combination of the reallocation of Ukraine's own budget resources, bilateral assistance, and using “money credits” from next year's portion of a €90 billion EU loan, Zelensky said.

articles.title: Putin’s Claims of Russian Battlefield Gains “Border on Hallucinations,” ISW Says - UNITED24 Media
articles.summary: Putin’s Claims of Russian Battlefield Gains “Border on Hallucinations,” ISW Says  UNITED24 MediaRussian Offensive Campaign Assessment, October 1, 2026  Institute for the Study of WarPutin claims Russia seized 1,301 square kilometers of Ukrainian territory in September, sharply diverging from  UkrinformOperation "Vivaldi" near Lyman may complicate Russia's advance on Sloviansk — ISW  Корабелов.ІНФОRussia lying about "encirclement" of Dobropillia, but still ...
articles.full_text:
Russian leader Vladimir Putin’s claims of major Russian battlefield gains in Ukraine in September “border on hallucinations,” according to the Institute for the Study of War (ISW), which assessed that Russian forces actually ended the month with a net territorial loss.
According to ISW on October 2, Putin claimed that Russian forces captured 1,301 square kilometers of Ukrainian territory in September. ISW’s battlefield data, however, showed that Russian forces suffered a net territorial loss of 80.81 square kilometers during the same period.
Putin made the claim during a meeting of the Valdai Discussion Club on October 1, saying Russian forces had brought 1,301 square kilometers of Ukrainian territory under their control in September—roughly 2.5 times more than in previous months.
ISW’s geolocated battlefield data showed a substantially different picture. The institute assessed that Russian forces captured 175.54 square kilometers during September, while Ukrainian forces regained 256.35 square kilometers.
That resulted in a net Russian territorial loss of 80.81 square kilometers over the course of the month, rather than the large territorial gain described by Putin.
The discrepancy becomes even larger when areas where Russian troops infiltrated but failed to establish control are included. Under that calculation, ISW assessed Russia’s net territorial losses in September at 175.18 square kilometers.
ISW said Putin’s claims about Russian battlefield progress were so disconnected from observed developments that they “border on hallucinations.”
The institute assessed that Putin’s statements are consistent with the Kremlin’s broader cognitive warfare efforts to portray Russian forces as advancing rapidly across the front and Ukrainian defenses as deteriorating.
ISW noted that it remains unclear whether Putin is aware of the discrepancy between the figures he publicly presents and observed battlefield developments.
The institute has previously assessed that senior Russian military officials have exaggerated territorial gains when reporting battlefield developments.
ISW has linked such discrepancies to what it describes as a deeply rooted practice within the Russian military command of concealing setbacks and presenting senior leadership with inflated reports of battlefield success.
During his Valdai remarks, Putin also claimed that Russian forces could seize the remaining Ukrainian-held areas of the Donetsk region sooner than Ukraine and European countries expect.
Earlier in September, ISW assessed that at Russia’s then-current rate of advance, its forces would need more than six years to capture the remaining Ukrainian-controlled territory in the Donetsk region, pushing the timeline to October 2032—well beyond Moscow’s stated goal of taking the entire region by the end of 2026.

articles.summary: North Korea says it test-fired an intermediate-range missile as tensions grow over mine blasts  AP NewsNorth Korea says it conducted intermediate-range strategic missile drill  reuters.comNorth Korea fires ballistic missile towards the sea, South Korea says  Al JazeeraNorth Korea launches ballistic missile after Seoul demands apology over wounded soldiers  theguardian.comNorth Korea launches ballistic missile 700 km. as hostilities heat up  The J...
articles.full_text:
SEOUL, South Korea (AP) — North Korea said Saturday it test-fired an intermediate-range ballistic missile that it claimed has maneuverable flight capabilities designed to evade missile defenses in South Korea and Japan. The latest test comes amid heightened tensions between the two Koreas over border land mine blasts.
Kim Yo Jong, the powerful sister of North Korean leader Kim Jong Un, said her brother supervised the test of the missile, which she described as strategic, implying it was designed to deliver nuclear weapons. She also said it could change its flight trajectory at low altitudes and was equipped with unspecified artificial intelligence capabilities that she claimed would make it highly difficult to intercept.
Japan’s military said the missile landed in waters outside its exclusive economic zone.
The South Korean military, which often accuses North Korea of exaggerating its military capabilities, did not immediately comment on Kim’s claims.
The North claims new missile capabilities
South Korea’s Joint Chiefs of Staff said early Saturday it detected the North Korean missile being launched from the eastern coastal Wonsan area and flying more than 700 kilometers (435 miles). Japan’s Defense Ministry later said it detected the missile flying about 680 kilometers (422 miles).
Kim argued in her statement that the differing flight details between the neighboring U.S. allies proved they couldn’t properly track the missile in flight.
“Whenever we applied the wavelike trajectory mode to missiles, the enemy failed to track the targets from their first skip points,” she said. “There is no way to avoid this attack.”
The launch came a day after she ridiculed South Korean demands for the North to apologize over the Sept. 21 land mine blasts, which occurred about 10 meters (11 yards) south of the countries’ military demarcation line, injuring three South Korean soldiers.
South Korea said a joint inspection of the site with the U.S.-led United Nations Command found the blasts were caused by mines planted by North Korea. The command later determined that the North violated the armistice agreement that ended fighting in the 1950-53 Korean War.
The South has also called on the North to halt its recent border fortification efforts, including the installation of mines and anti-tank barriers, which have accelerated after Kim Jong Un in 2024 abandoned his government’s long-standing goal of reconciliation with the South and declared Seoul a permanent adversary.
Kim Yo Jong, possibly the second-most powerful figure in Pyongyang, dismissed Seoul’s demands over the mine blasts as “utterly pathetic” on Friday, saying the North intends to cut ties with the South forever. In a statement on Sept. 30, she denied North Korean responsibility for the blasts and threatened to retaliate if South Korea fires on North Korean troops fortifying the border.
North Korea has upped its weapons tests
Saturday’s launch at Wonsan was the latest in a series of North Korean military displays in recent weeks, including missile tests, live-fire exercises and the commissioning of a new warship, as Kim Jong Un continues to flaunt his growing nuclear program despite U.S. calls to revive diplomacy.
Wonsan was also the site where the North on Sept. 20 tested what state media described as a hypersonic missile system, part of a broad range of weapons North Korea has developed in recent years that are designed to overwhelm missile defenses in South Korea and Japan. The various hypersonic systems tested by the North have included solid-fuel intermediate-range missiles that were first unveiled in 2024.
The South’s joint chiefs said Saturday the military stepped up surveillance and vigilance for possible further launches from the North and was closely sharing information with the United States and Japan.
Seoul’s presidential national security office called for North Korea to immediately halt its repeated ballistic launches, calling them a violation of U.N. Security Council sanctions and a “serious act that does nothing to help manage the current situation.”
The U.S. Pacific Command said the launch “does not pose an immediate threat to U.S. personnel or territory, or to our allies.”
Kim Jong Un has largely abandoned diplomacy with Washington and Seoul since his nuclear negotiations with U.S. President Donald Trump collapsed in 2019, and he has made Moscow the new focus of his foreign policy, sending thousands of troops and large quantities of weapons to support President Vladimir Putin’s war in Ukraine.
Following years of intensified testing, Kim now has an extensive arsenal of nuclear-capable missiles, including long-range weapons potentially capable of reaching the U.S. mainland and shorter-range systems that threaten South Korea and Japan.
Trump in August scaled back a major military exercise with South Korea in an apparent effort to restart diplomacy with Kim, who has condemned such drills as rehearsals for invasion.
North Korea has so far rebuffed Trump’s outreach. It says Washington must first abandon its “hostile policy” — a term Pyongyang has traditionally used to describe U.S.-led sanctions and joint U.S.-South Korean military exercises — and drop denuclearization as a precondition for talks.
__ Associated Press writer Yuri Kageyama in Tokyo contributed to this report.

articles.summary: UK-Iranian dual national arrested over RAF Fairford released on bail  BBCWhat we know and don’t know about how Iran uses asymmetric warfare  AP NewsHow RAF Fairford in a Quiet Corner of England Became a U.S.-Iran Flashpoint  The New York TimesDual U.K.-Iranian national released on bail over suspected plot against U.S.-run military base  NBC NewsMan arrested in Fairford air base investigation released on bail  reuters.com
articles.full_text:
A UK-Iranian dual national arrested on suspicion of preparation of terrorist acts in connection with an incident at RAF Fairford has been released on bail.
The 25-year-old man was arrested in the London borough of Westminster on Thursday. Searches of two properties in the same area have now finished.
A major incident was declared and dozens of homes were evacuated after police were alerted to three "suspicious vehicles" near the airbase in Gloucestershire last weekend.
Five other men in their twenties were arrested and were subsequently released on police bail. All five were UK nationals from London.
The investigation into the circumstances surrounding the events are continuing, police said.
Last weekend, the five men aged between 23 and 25 were arrested in the early hours of the morning after vehicles were reported to be travelling towards the base operated by the US Air Force (USAF), sparking a major security incident.
The BBC understands that one of the men had dialled 999 himself, about an hour before a local farmer alerted police to a "large group" of masked men near the vehicles.
They were arrested on suspicion of explosives offences and later on suspicion of preparing a terrorist act, before being released on bail on Monday in what police called an "investigative decision" that was "grounded in experience and strategy".
Prime Minister Andy Burnham chaired a Cobra meeting that afternoon in response. He later said there were "strong indications" that Iran had played a part in the incident, but did not provide any more details.
Tehran has strongly denied any involvement. The Iranian embassy in London said on Monday that it "categorically rejects and strongly condemns" what it called "unfounded and malicious speculations" linking Iran to the incident.
RAF Fairford has been used as a forward operating location by the US Air Force (USAF) for decades.
In recent months, US bombers have taken off from the base for the Middle East, after the UK approved a US request to use it for defensive strikes on Iran.
In July, Iran said "any base used for aggression against Iranian territory constitutes a legitimate target for our forces".
Late on Monday, US Secretary of State Marco Rubio told a TV show that it was clear a "foreign actor" had been involved in events over the weekend.
Without providing evidence or giving further details, he told Fox News network's "Hannity" programme: "What happened, what almost happened, what could have happened in the UK over the weekend is a very serious situation. It's one that clearly involves the hands of a foreign actor."
Speaking earlier at the Oval Office, US President Donald Trump said he would not have let the five men arrested out on bail, and that he was "surprised" they had been released.
"We know everything about them, we would not have released them," he said, adding that the UK had worked with the US "very closely" on this.

articles.title: Second Kyiv bridge hit in two days as Russia targets Dnipro crossings - Euronews.com
articles.summary: Second Kyiv bridge hit in two days as Russia targets Dnipro crossings  Euronews.comRussia hits second major bridge in Ukraine's capital Kyiv  BBCUkraine war briefing: Russian attacks on Kyiv bridges cause traffic chaos  The GuardianRussia strikes another major bridge in Kyiv as attacks on Ukrainian capital escalate  CNNRussia bombs Kyiv bridge in new tactic to carve city in two  The Telegraph
articles.full_text:
With the Northern Bridge's traffic blocked a day after jet-powered drones forced the Southern Bridge shut, two of the eight Dnipro crossings joining Kyiv's halves are now disrupted.
A Russian strike hit Kyiv's Northern Bridge on Saturday, halting traffic from the left bank to the right and deepening a transport crisis that began when the Southern Bridge was shut a day earlier.
Mayor Vitali Klitschko announced the strike on Telegram after a drone alert in the capital. "Northern Bridge has been hit," he wrote. "Emergency services are heading to the scene."
He later reported damage to the road surface and to the overhead wires that power trolleybuses on the bridge. "Traffic across the bridge from the left bank to the right bank is currently blocked," he said.
The strike is the latest in a series aimed at the crossings over the Dnipro, the river that separates Kyiv's eastern and western districts. Eight bridges connect the two sides, and city officials say the campaign is "tearing Kyiv apart".
The Southern Bridge, a cable-stayed span and one of the city's main crossings, was closed on Friday after waves of fast, jet-powered drones struck. Officials said it had been hit several times since Thursday. Movement on another bridge was also restricted.
The closures brought severe congestion across the city. Cars and buses stood in long queues on major roads as drivers looked for other ways across, and some commuters had to finish their journeys on foot.
Klitschko warned on Friday that the capital should now be on a war footing.
Since Russia's full-scale invasion in February 2022, the war has largely been fought on the ground in the east, and Kyiv has mostly been spared the destruction seen near the front line.

articles.title: Iran gearing up for 'major round of fighting' with US, says source - thenationalnews.com
articles.summary: Iran gearing up for 'major round of fighting' with US, says source  thenationalnews.comPolitics  The EconomistHormuz and Yemen: Iran offers de-escalation at a price others will pay  Al JazeeraUN ambassador Waltz says Iran was not negotiating ‘in good faith’ to end war | Trump administration  The GuardianIranian Delegation to Meet Mediators in New York: Source  تسنیم
articles.full_text:
Iran is preparing for a renewed major round of fighting with the US, even as diplomatic efforts in New York failed to produce a breakthrough.
A third US aircraft carrier strike group, the USS Theodore Roosevelt, is heading to the Middle East, signalling Washington's military readiness.
Iran has proposed transferring its 60 per cent enriched uranium stockpile to a third party as part of a phased diplomatic road map.
The Houthis, aided by Iranian operatives, have seized Yemen's western coast and are pressing an offensive on Taiz, threatening regional stability.
"The door to diplomacy remains open and has not been closed. But assessments in Iran are that the war is resuming," a source in Tehran said.
Iran is preparing for a “major round of fighting”, a source in Tehran said on Saturday, as diplomatic efforts falter and the US administration considers its next steps.
The two sides met in New York last month to find common ground as a prelude to full negotiations to end seven months of conflict, but no breakthrough emerged after several meetings.
US President Donald Trump and Iranian officials have since signalled that they are preparing for a resumption of the war, with Iran’s Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi saying his country would fight even if it meant an “apocalyptic” war.
“The military option [for the US] has not been abandoned, and this is clear to the Iranians,” said the source in Tehran. “But the Iranians are also preparing for a major round of fighting and have the capabilities to do so”.
A US official told The National on Thursday that a third aircraft carrier strike group, the USS Theodore Roosevelt, is en route to Central Command's area of operations, which spans the Middle East.
Axios later reported that Mr Trump’s top national security officials held a “secret meeting” at Camp David to discuss the next steps in the Iran war and Washington’s approach to the Iran-backed Houthi offensive in Yemen.
Vice President JD Vance chaired the meeting at the presidential retreat, the US news outlet added, citing people familiar with the discussions.
Yemeni rebels have been launching attacks on the strategic city of Taiz in south-western Yemen after taking control of the western coast. The offensive, even if it does not succeed, has put significant pressure on government forces and is preventing them from launching counter-attacks to regain areas overlooking the Bab Al Mandeb strait.
The rebels, who seized the coast with the help of Iranian operatives according to multiple Yemeni and Iranian sources, have not yet disrupted shipping through the waterway. However, the Tehran source said this did not mean there would be no action there.
“The cautious approach to Bab Al Mandeb so far does not mean it will be incapable of acting later,” claimed the source. “Likewise, the aerial blockade imposed on Iran does not mean Tehran will simply stand by and watch. Iran’s security cannot be separated from the security of the region.”
In New York, Mr Araghchi said his country had conveyed to the US, through Qatar, a firm seven-day plan to resolve the stand-off over the Strait of Hormuz, with the waterway expected to reopen on the sixth day if the agreed steps were implemented.
The US subsequently sent a counterproposal, which Iran has yet to respond to but appears unlikely to accept, having insisted that its own proposal was the only way forward.
According to sources in Tehran, during the latest talks Iran has also proposed transferring its stockpile of uranium enriched to 60 per cent to a third party as part of its latest plan to break the diplomatic deadlock with the US.
The proposal envisages a phased process in which the stockpile would first be diluted before being transferred out of Iran under mechanisms recognised by the International Atomic Energy Agency.
The third-party transfer goes beyond Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian's public comments that Tehran was prepared to dilute its 60 per cent enriched uranium and submit the process to verification. The mechanism revives and expands an idea discussed during earlier negotiations mediated by Oman and, the source said, shortly before the war began on February 28.
US and Iranian officials have said that Iran wants Washington to take concrete steps before Tehran fully reopens the Strait of Hormuz, reversing the sequence in previous negotiations, where agreements were negotiated first and implemented afterwards. Washington, however, wants Iran to reopen the strategic waterway first.
“The door to diplomacy remains open and has not been closed. But assessments in Iran are that the war is resuming,” the Tehran source claimed.

articles.summary: EU pushes Ukraine for further reforms to unlock funding  Financial TimesEurope is losing patience with Ukraine’s demands  UnHerdUkraine's 2026 budget, defence needs are covered, EU says  ReutersUkraine’s war chest is running low at the worst possible moment  politico.euUkraine nets 2.9 billion euros from EU after passing reforms  The Kyiv Independent
articles.full_text:
Simply sign up to the War in Ukraine myFT Digest -- delivered directly to your inbox.
Brussels has rebuffed Ukraine’s request for additional financial support this year, demanding that Kyiv implement promised reforms before receiving further EU funding.
The decision comes as Ukraine grapples with intensified Russian attacks on civilian infrastructure, while its parliament struggles to pass the reforms required to unlock support from the EU and other donors.
This summer, Kyiv identified an additional $27bn in military needs and asked the European Commission to help cover the gap by bringing forward tranches from a €90bn EU loan agreed late last year.
That loan was intended to cover most of Ukraine’s financing needs in 2026 and 2027, allocating up to €45bn each year if certain reform milestones were met. However, only €15.7bn of this has been disbursed this year, partly due to delays in complying with reform requirements.
President Volodymyr Zelenskyy has said further funding is urgently needed, in part to boost production of drones and interceptors as Moscow intensifies its aerial attacks on Ukrainian cities and critical infrastructure ahead of the winter.
But Brussels rejected the request to frontload 2027 funding, instead pressing Kyiv to meet conditions that could unlock about €34bn in EU support this year.
In a joint statement on Thursday, Ukraine and the European Commission said they had “identified the means to cover Ukraine’s budget and defence needs for 2026. We have also reconfirmed the steps needed to ensure their timely release.”
The reforms Ukraine must deliver to receive the funds include the abolition of a VAT exemption for small parcels and the introduction of new taxation rules for digital platforms.
Both measures have passed in parliament, but include a controversial amendment that weakens the rules governing politically exposed persons (PEPs), which had been requested by the EU to strengthen anti-corruption efforts. That amendment, if signed into law, could threaten Ukraine’s compliance with the conditions attached to EU funding.
European commissioners Valdis Dombrovskis and Marta Kos wrote a letter to the Speaker of Ukraine’s parliament, underscoring that additional financial assistance in 2026 was still available to Ukraine if it fulfilled the requested reforms.
“Avoiding any weakening of Ukraine’s framework on PEPs” was “essential”, they wrote in the letter, which was seen by the FT.
In an interview with the FT on Thursday, Zelenskyy pushed back against media reports of tense discussions with Commission president Ursula von der Leyen over reform conditions.
“We had a very good meeting with Ursula and with her team, and she understands that they have to help Ukraine,” he said.
Europe should help close Kyiv’s financing gap “because we are defending them”, he added. “They have to do it for them also, not only for us.”
He said he had told von der Leyen that wartime pressures meant reforms could not always proceed according to a normal timetable.
“We have to defend [ourselves] now, and some decisions, financial decisions, you can’t wait ,” he said. “Because it’s a question of our stability.”
The Commission is also assessing Ukraine’s yet-uncovered financing needs for 2027, which officials said could total about €70bn in military and budgetary support. The assessment is expected to be presented to EU leaders meeting in mid-October.
Ukraine is in discussions with the IMF about further disbursements from its $8bn programme, a review of which is due later this year. Those disbursements are contingent on funding agreements from the EU and Kyiv’s other allies that will help cover Ukraine’s financial needs in 2027.

articles.summary: Putin says all weapons 'on agenda' if Russia's Kaliningrad attacked  Euronews.comPutin says Russia will use ‘all weapons’ in its arsenal if any of its territory is attacked  AP NewsPutin warns Russia is prepared to use ‘all weapons,’ including nuclear, to protect Kaliningrad  CNNPutin says ‘all weapons at disposal’ if there’s an attack on Russia – as it happened  theguardian.comKaliningrad is just Putin’s red herring  The Hill
articles.full_text:
Russia would consider using "all types of weapons" if its exclave of Kaliningrad was attacked, Russian President Vladimir Putin said Thursday, while insisting that Moscow had "no intention of attacking anyone."
Russian President Vladimir Putin threatened the West that he would use "all weapons" in its arsenal — including nuclear — if Kaliningrad were attacked.
Putin comments came as tensions mounted over Kaliningrad — Russia's heavily militarised territory that borders Poland, Lithuania and the Baltic Sea.
"If it comes to a direct attack on the Russian Federation... then, of course, the question of the Russian Federation deploying all types of weapons at our country's disposal will inevitably and immediately be on the agenda. This is inevitable," Putin said at the annual Valdai forum.
In recent months, NATO countries have conducted several military exercises along Kaliningrad's borders. That prompted Moscow to issue a statement condemning what it called "provocative statements and actions of the North Atlantic Alliance's leadership and NATO member states".
NATO in turn has denounced Russia's "threat of force, including any irresponsible nuclear rhetoric".
On Thursday, Putin once again condemned the "successive military exercises in the Baltic Sea" and the "attempts to intercept" Russian vessels.
"All this constitutes an escalation," he said.
"We have no intention of attacking anyone — neither in 2029, nor in 2030, nor in 2050," Putin said.
"However, if we face aggression, we will be compelled to respond. Citizens of European countries need to clearly understand this," he added.

articles.summary: Map shows Ukraine's major September gains as Russian casualties hit 2026 high  NewsweekRussian Offensive Campaign Assessment, October 1, 2026  Institute for the Study of WarThe Russia-Ukraine War Report Card, Sept. 30, 2026  Russia MattersPutin’s Claims of Russian Battlefield Gains “Border on Hallucinations,” ISW Says  UNITED24 MediaPutin claims Russia seized 1,301 square kilometers of Ukrainian territory in September, sharply diverging from  Ukr...
articles.full_text:
Russia suffered its highest monthly losses of the year in September but gained no territory in return, according to the Institute for the Study of War (ISW), whose latest map outlines the state of the frontline.
Ukraine’s armed forces said on Thursday that Russia had suffered 46,000 casualties last month, while the Washington, D.C.-based think tank gave its assessment of how the battlefield has shifted over the last six months.
This has coincided with a Ukrainian counteroffensive, "Operation Vivaldi," in the Lyman sector of the Donetsk oblast, which has thwarted Moscow’s attempts to capture the "Fortress Belt" of cities critical to holding the Donbas region.
High Russian troop losses for negligible territorial gains add pressure on President Vladimir Putin amid speculation about a widespread mobilization to replenish troops.
Newsweek reached out to the Russian defense ministry for comment.
How Many Troops Did Russia Lose?
It is tricky to ascertain losses in the Ukraine war, with both sides tight-lipped about casualty figures. Moscow has not updated its death toll from the 6,000 it revealed in the first year of the war.
But evidence suggests Russian losses are rising amid minimal battlefield gains.
NATO Secretary General Mark Rutte said last month that Russia had over 40,000 casualties per month, referring to those who have been killed and injured.
This was up from the 30,000-a-month figure he gave in June, the same month in which the British government said intelligence indicated nearly 500,000 Russian soldiers had been killed, as it assessed that the Russian military is “going backwards on the battlefield.”
The September figure from Ukraine’s armed forces, released Thursday, was its highest monthly tally of the year—up from 42,860 in July and a marked increase from January’s 32,980.
Meanwhile, the ISW said it was unclear how much territory Russian forces lost the same month due to the uncertainty about when Ukrainian forces liberated territory near Lyman.
“Russian forces continue to sustain significant personnel losses while achieving extremely limited or even net negative territorial gains,” the think tank said, noting how Russia's recruits are not enough to replace the losses. The Kremlin has repeatedly denied it planned a widespread mobilization.
The ISW also said that between March and September, Russian troops lost almost 115 square miles of territory.
Operation Vivaldi started in early summer and has liberated at least 147 square kilometers (56 square miles), according to Ukraine’s 3rd Army Corps commander, Andriy Biletskyi, who has touted the use of drones, robots and deception as contributing to the gains.
As its map shows, the ISW said it had evidence that Russian forces seized 175.54 square kilometers (67 square miles) last month but lost 256.35 square kilometers (98 square miles) of territory in September, for a total loss of 80.81 square kilometers (30 square miles).
Meanwhile, the Vivaldi operation near Lyman could complicate Russia's offensive toward the fortress-belt city of Sloviansk, which has worried Russian military bloggers who offer an unvarnished view of Moscow’s war effort.
The ISW cited the military bloggers' concerns that the Ukrainian counteroffensive may stop Russian plans to assault the Fortress Belt cities from the front.
